name: Aakash Tyagi
thesis_title: Investigations on feedstock handling for powder-based additive manufacturing
abstract:
Powder-based additive manufacturing processes, including directed energy deposition (DED) and powder bed fusion (PBF), enable the fabrication of complex metal components. However, part quality depends on powder behaviour and its control during spreading and delivery. This work investigates powder characterization and develops powder-handling systems for these processes.
An experimental device was developed to measure the coefficient of restitution (COR) and investigate particle impact behaviour, providing information for selecting contact parameters in discrete element method (DEM) simulations. For PBF, a gravity-based, non-contact spreading system initially used a vibrating hopper. The effects of vibration frequency, spreading speed, and stand-off distance were evaluated through voidage, spreading efficiency, and powder distribution uniformity. A subsequent design incorporated a rotating slotted shaft to regulate powder discharge and was tested on flat and textured substrates.
For DED, a non-pneumatic delivery system with a two-stage rotating-disc distributor was optimized to achieve a powder focal diameter of 2.5 mm. SS316 and Al?O? powders were delivered at different ratios without premixing or carrier gas. Deposited coatings were assessed through elemental analysis, microhardness, wear, and corrosion testing.
Together, these developments offer alternative approaches to powder characterization, non-contact spreading, and multi-material delivery for metal components and composite coatings.
keywords: Discrete Element Method; Additive manufacturing; Directed energy deposition;  Powder bed fusion; Composite coatings; Tribology; Advanced manufacturing processes; Micromachining; Surface modification; wear testing.

name: ABHIMANYU SINGH
thesis_title: Design and Optimization of Battery-pack System for Electric Vehicle Subjected to Mechanical Loading Conditions.
abstract: My research focuses on computational mechanics, finite element analysis, and simulation-driven design and optimization of advanced battery systems, with emphasis on mechanical safety, thermo-mechanical behaviour, thermal management, and failure prediction. My Ph.D. research at IIT Guwahati investigates the structural and thermal performance of lithium-ion battery cells and packs under mechanical loading conditions. The work involves developing homogenized anisotropic constitutive models incorporating orthotropic elasticity, anisotropic plasticity, and ductile damage to predict damage initiation and failure of pouch cells under in-plane and out-of-plane compression. Sequentially coupled thermo-mechanical analysis, dynamic indentation, crashworthiness assessment, and vibration-fatigue analysis are also performed to evaluate battery safety and structural reliability. My industry experience at ideaForge Technology Ltd. extends this research to advanced lithium-ion and solid-state battery systems for UAV and aerospace applications, including cell, module, and pack design, thermal management, and thermal runaway mitigation. I also conduct finite element heat-transfer simulations and experimental battery testing, including charge–discharge characterization, capacity assessment, cycle-life evaluation, and profile testing. Furthermore, sensitivity analysis, surrogate modelling, artificial neural networks, and multi-objective optimization are employed to identify critical design parameters and improve battery-system performance, safety, and reliability.
keywords: Lithium-Ion Batteries; Battery Cell and Pack Design; Finite Element Analysis; Anisotropic Plasticity; Ductile Damage; Thermo-Mechanical Analysis; Thermal Runaway; Thermal Management; Battery Safety; Mechanical Abuse; Crashworthiness; Experimental Battery Testing; UAV Battery Systems; Design Optimization; Artificial Neural Networks

name: Abhishek Mondal
thesis_title: Development and GPU Acceleration of an Unstructured Finite Volume Solver for Compressible Flows Solvers
abstract: Development of an in-house unstructured-grid finite-volume solver, written in C/C++, for compressible flow computations. Multiple approximate Riemann solvers (Roe, AUSM, AUSM+, and LLF/Rusanov) and implemented and provides second-order spatial accuracy through least-squares gradient reconstruction with slope limiters. A diffusion-regulation framework is first presented unifying a broad class of entropy-violating upwind schemes under a single formulation with better contact resolution. A complementary diffusion-lowering mechanism sharpens the resolution of shocks and viscous boundary-layer interactions. The solver is parallelized with custom CUDA C kernels, including parallel reductions for global time-stepping and residuals using cuBLAS. OpenACC  is also implemented for multi-core CPU support. It achieves speedups of about 10× on multi-core CPUs and about 40× on GPUs relative to the serial baseline. Validation against standard 1D/2D benchmarks (Sod and Lax shock tubes, double Mach reflection, and 2D Riemann problems) is followed by application to subsonic inviscid and viscous flow over cylinders and airfoils. Separately, vortex-induced vibration (VIV) is analyzed in OpenFOAM using a cylinder-attached, non-inertial reference frame on a static mesh.
keywords: Compressible Flow; High Performance Computing; Shock Waves; Finite Volume Method; Inviscid Flow; Viscid Flow; Vortex Induced Vibrations

name: Abhishek Punia
thesis_title: AI-Based Chatter Detection in Machining: Data-Driven and Physics-Guided Learning Frameworks
abstract:
Machining chatter is a self-excited vibration that compromises surface quality, dimensional accuracy, tool life, and productivity. This doctoral research develops artificial intelligence (AI)-based frameworks for accurate, computationally efficient, and data-efficient chatter detection in turning, with emphasis on robustness and generalization across machining conditions.

The first investigation uses experimentally acquired cutting-force signals and systematic statistical feature optimization to identify a compact feature set for machine-learning classification. The second develops a non-contact, vision-based approach using machined-surface images. Customized ResNet50 transfer-learning architectures are evaluated with different image magnifications, augmentation strategies, and progressive fine-tuning to enable effective learning from limited data.

The third investigation integrates mechanistic simulations of regenerative machining dynamics with experimental force signals through physics-guided deep learning. Simulated and measured signals are represented using the short-time Fourier transform, while teacher–student knowledge transfer aims to improve detection under limited experimental data. Complementary ongoing work explores autoencoder-based representation learning from combined simulated and experimental signals.

Together, these studies combine experimental machining, signal processing, computer vision, dynamic modeling, and deep learning to advance intelligent process monitoring and support reliable, efficient, and more autonomous manufacturing.
keywords: Physics-Guided Machine Learning; Intelligent Manufacturing; Machining Chatter Detection; Machine Learning and Deep Learning; Machining Dynamics; Condition Monitoring; Computer Vision for Manufacturing; Transfer Learning; Signal Processing; Simulation-Assisted Learning

name: ABHISHEK RAJ
thesis_title: Numerical study on dynamics of viscoelastic drop impact on a solid surface
abstract:
I am a Mechanical Engineering researcher with a background in fluid mechanics and expertise in computational fluid dynamics (CFD), multiphase flows and viscoelastic fluid dynamics. I completed my B.Tech. in Mechanical Engineering from JIS College of Engineering in 2018 and pursued master and doctoral research (Thesis submitted) at the Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati.

My doctoral work focuses on the numerical investigation of viscoelastic droplet impact on solid surfaces. It examines the effects of inertia, viscosity, surface tension, and polymer-induced elastic stresses on droplet spreading, recoil, rebound, coalescence, and fluid entrapment. I have also investigated thermal effects, successive droplet interactions, and evaporation.

I have experience developing numerical models using the open-source CFD framework Basilisk, the VOF method for interface tracking, and the Oldroyd-B constitutive model with the log-conformation formulation. My research activities include computational modelling, numerical simulations, parameter studies, post-processing, and interpretation of results.

My technical interests include CFD, fluid mechanics, heat transfer, multiphase and numerical methods. I aim to apply my analytical, computational and problem-solving skills to industrial research and development while contributing to teaching, student mentoring, and collaborative academic research. I am interested in interdisciplinary applications where computational modelling supports engineering analysis, innovation and problem-solving.
keywords: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD); Multiphase Flow; Fluid Mechanics; Viscoelastic Fluids; Drop Impact Dynamics; Heat Transfer; Evaporation; Numerical Simulation; Research and Development (R&D); Engineering Education

name: Abinash Baruah
thesis_title: Multiscale Phenomena in Perovskite LEDs: Coupled Interplay of Ion Migration, Dielectric Relaxation, and Trap-Assisted Degradation
abstract:
My research expertise lies in semiconductor devices, optoelectronics, thin-film materials, and device physics, with a focus on understanding charge transport, dielectric relaxation, ion migration, and device reliability. I completed my PhD research at IIT Guwahati, where I investigated the performance and degradation mechanisms of metal halide perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs). My work involved device fabrication, electrical and optical characterization, impedance spectroscopy, electric modulus analysis, deep-level transient spectroscopy (DLTS), and time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL). I developed physical models to understand ionic transport, grain-boundary polarization, trap states, and their influence on device performance and operational stability.
Currently, as a Project Engineer at IIT Kanpur, I am working on the development of flexible organic solar cells on conventional and paper-based substrates, with an emphasis on thin-film deposition, interface engineering, device optimization, and scalable fabrication techniques, including printing-based processes.
My technical skills include semiconductor device fabrication, photolithography, spin coating, thermal evaporation, thin-film characterization, electrical measurements, impedance analysis, data processing, and physics-based modelling. I have experience in experimental design, material optimization, scientific research, technical documentation, and interdisciplinary problem-solving, with research interests extending to flexible electronics, printed photovoltaics, and emerging semiconductor technologies.
keywords: Semiconductor Device Physics; Perovskite Light-Emitting Diodes (PeLEDs); Organic Solar Cells; Flexible and Printed Electronics; Thin-Film Fabrication; Optoelectronic Devices; Ion Migration; Impedance Spectroscopy; Trap-State Characterization; Device Degradation and Reliability; Photolithography; Thin-Film Characterization

name: Aditi Paul
thesis_title: High-Performance VLSI Architectures for Continuous-Flow Spectral Transform Processing for 5G and Other DSP Applications
abstract: The evolution of Fifth-Generation (5G) New Radio (NR) standards and increasing Digital Signal Processing (DSP) demands require efficient hardware for spectral transforms. This thesis presents high-performance VLSI architectures for continuous-flow Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT), and Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), addressing trade-offs in throughput, latency, area, power, and numerical accuracy. Initially, a high-throughput, low-latency 256-point FFT architecture integrated with a Power Spectral Density (PSD) computation unit is developed. An optimized Radix-16 256-point real-valued FFT architecture is then proposed, exploiting conjugate symmetry to reduce complexity and area. Building on these designs, a memory-based continuous-flow 4096-point FFT/IFFT processor for 5G NR achieves 4.0 GS/s throughput and 2.42 ?s latency at 250 MHz, using 16 parallel data streams with 16-bit word length. A continuous-flow in-place reordering scheme generates ordered outputs without interrupting processing. To improve numerical accuracy, Half-Unit-Biased (HUB) quantization is incorporated into butterfly, rotator, trivial-rotator, and CORDIC-based processing units. The proposed HUB-based truncation and scaling configuration improves Signal-to-Quantization-Noise Ratio (SQNR) by 7.8 dB over the 4096-point FFT architecture. Finally, a continuous-flow STFT processor using a time-multiplexed hop-FFT core is developed for non-stationary signal analysis. These contributions support high-throughput, low-latency spectral processing for 5G and other DSP applications.
keywords: DSP Hardware Architecture; FFT/IFFT Hardware; CORDIC and CSD units; Hardware aware quantization; ASIC; FPGA; Synthesizable RTL; Verilog/System Verilog; Synopsys Design Compiler, VCS, formality; Cadence Genus, NC Launch, Innovus; Timing constraints

name: AISHWARYA VIJAYAKUMAR
thesis_title: Targeting hIAPP aggregation: phage display discovery of novel peptide inhibitors
abstract: The ?-cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans secrete both insulin and human islet amyloid polypeptide (hIAPP). The aggregation of hIAPP, which results in ?-cell death, is a pathological hallmark of type 2 diabetes. The death of ?-cells results in reduced insulin secretion. hIAPP comprises an amyloidogenic core spanning residues 20-29. Previous studies have shown that within an hIAPP dimer, the 23-27 residue stretch (FGAIL) forms a transient parallel ?-sheet, before the onset of aggregation. By screening a phage library against the FGAIL stretch, we identified a novel inhibitor which delayed the aggregation of hIAPP in a dose-dependent manner. The inhibitor protected cells from the cytotoxic effect of hIAPP aggregation in vitro and exhibited good serum stability. Since certain residues outside the FGAIL stretch are also responsible for hIAPP aggregation, we also identified an aggregation inhibitor by screening a phage library against full length hIAPP.
keywords: Phage Display; Aggregation Inhibition; Solid Phase Peptide Synthesis; HPLC; MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry; CD Spectroscopy; Fluorescence Spectroscopy; Serum Stability; Cytotoxicity

name: Akash Dilip Kamble
discipline: School of Energy Science and Engineering
thesis_title: DESIGN, DEVELOPMENT AND PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS OF ADVANCED PHOTOVOLTAIC–THERMAL (PV/T) COLLECTORS
abstract: This study presents the development and experimental evaluation of Hilbert-based photovoltaic–thermal (PV/T) collectors through distance-field-guided absorber selection and flow-topology optimization. Initially, four geometrical configurations, namely vertical and horizontal serpentine, rectangular spiral, and Hilbert patterns, were comparatively analysed using probability density function (PDF), cumulative distribution function (CDF), and spatial distance metrics in MATLAB. Based on their spatial distribution characteristics, the Hilbert geometry was selected for further experimental investigation. Subsequently, three flow topologies, namely sequential, multi-branch, and combined flow paths, were developed while retaining the same Hilbert-based absorber geometry. The sequential (SISO: single-inlet single-outlet) and multi-branch (MIMO: multi-inlet multi-outlet) configurations were experimentally evaluated under outdoor conditions against an uncooled PV module. Thermal imaging and surface-temperature distribution analysis demonstrated improved cooling performance, reducing the average PV surface temperature from 49°C (uncooled PV) to 43°C (SISO) and 40°C (MIMO). The SISO configuration achieved a maximum average thermal efficiency of 62.38%, whereas MIMO exhibited superior electrical and exergetic efficiencies of 12.48% and 13.89%, respectively. The findings demonstrate the potential of Hilbert-based PV/T collectors, highlighting the influence of flow topology on thermal and electrical performance.
keywords: Solar photovoltaic-thermal systems (PV/T); Heat transfer enhancement; Hilbert curve; Flow topology; Thermal uniformity; Sustainability

name: Akshita Kanwar
discipline: School of Interdisciplinary Studies and Sustainability
thesis_title: Construction of cellulolytic chimera for lignocellulosic bioethanol production
abstract:
Glycoside hydrolases (GHs) are enzymes with high specificity possessing the ability to cleave the glycosidic bonds present in the polysaccharides of complex nature such as cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin constituting the lignocellulose. Cellulases belong to the family of GHs. The present research focuses on the construction of a bi-functional cellulosic chimera and its structural elucidation and biochemical characterization. The genes encoding ?-glucosidase from GH family 1 (AtGH1) and endoglucanase from GH family 8 (AtGH8) were fused by using a natural linker from the cellulosomal gene celH from Acetivibrio thermocellus and expressed as a soluble protein of 95 kDa size [1].
The chimera showed maximum endoglucanase activity (5900 µmol min-1µmol of protein-1) using 1%, w/v CMC-Na at 72ºC and pH 5.8 and ?-glucosidase activity (4800 µmol min-1 µmol of protein-1) using 1 mM p-Nitrophenyl glucopyranoside at 68ºC, pH 5.8 (50 mM citrate phosphate buffer). The protein melting temperature (Tm) of chimera analyzed by Dynamic Light Scattering was 75°C. The 3D structure of chimera was predicted by using AlphaFold2 Colab web server. The overall modelled protein showed a two-domain fusion displaying a classic (?/?)-TIM barrel fold for the ?-glucosidase module linked to an (?/?)6 barrel catalytic endoglucanase module. The surface view of chimera showed the active-site residues for both ?-glucosidase (Glu189 and Glu378) and endoglucanase (Glu 553 and Asp 610). The secondary structure composition of chimera deduced by circular dichroism showed 49% ?-helices and 18% ?-strands, while Psi-Pred web server showed 42% of ?-helix, 12% of ?-sheets. Molecular docking revealed that ?-glucosidase module shows binding with pNPG, glucose, cellobiose and the endoglucanase module shows binding with cellotetraose, cellopentaose and cellohexaose with binding free energy (?G) of -7.6, -6.71, -6.8 and -6.9, -7.0, -7.2 kcal/mol, respectively. Molecular dynamic simulation of both unbound and docked AtGH1-L1-AtGH8-cellobiose and AtGH1-L1-AtGH8-cellotetroase was compared which revealed stability and compactness of docked complexes. The RMSD profile of chimera was 0.7 nm at 10 ns and remained stable thereafter. The radius of gyration (Rg) of chimera, achieved stability and compactness at 3.07 nm. The average SASA of chimera remained fairly stable with an average value of 370 nm2 till 100 ns. Dynamic light scattering analysis of chimera at 1 mg/mL showed a hydrodynamic diameter of 25 nm confirming its monomeric and stable state.
keywords: Cellulases; Glycoside hydrolases; chimera; bioethanol

name: Amarnath Kumar
thesis_title: Development of Wireless Power Transmission for Aerial Vehicle Charging
abstract: Microwave wireless power transfer (MWPT) offers a promising route to powering remote sensors, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and inaccessible electronic systems without physical connections. Its practical use, however, is held back by beam spreading, low power density at the receiver, and poor RF-to-DC conversion efficiency. This research tackles these problems with three complementary contributions. First, graded-permittivity Fresnel zone plate (FZP) lenses are designed and developed to focus microwave energy. A spatially varying dielectric profile improves focusing gain, reduces losses, and gives a compact, low-profile alternative to conventional lenses. Second, metamaterial reflectors are engineered to redirect and concentrate incident electromagnetic waves. This improves power capture at the receiving end and makes the link less sensitive to alignment. Third, high-efficiency RF–DC converters (rectennas) are developed with optimized impedance matching networks and rectifying circuits. These keep conversion efficiency high across a range of input power levels and loads. The proposed components are characterized through simulation and experimental measurement, and they show clear gains in end-to-end power transfer efficiency. Together, these advances support more efficient, compact, and reliable microwave energy harvesting and wireless power systems for next-generation self-powered and battery-less applications.
keywords: Microwave wireless power transfer; Graded-permittivity Fresnel zone plate lens; Metamaterial reflector; RF–DC converter (rectenna); Energy harvesting

name: Ambuj Kumar
thesis_title: Assessment of Physicochemical and Dielectric Properties of Transformer Oils in Reclamation and Retro filling Processes
abstract: Moisture is a principal threat to transformer insulation, reducing breakdown strength and accelerating the degradation of oil and cellulose pressboard. Natural ester oil (NEO), increasingly adopted as a sustainable alternative to mineral oil (MO), can dissolve far more water, so drying methods must be effective for both oil types. This thesis investigates water-stable zirconium metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), namely MOF-801-P and UiO-66, as adsorbents for drying MO and NEO. Water uptake was characterised through sorption isotherms, and moisture removal was quantified in fresh and oxidised oils by monitoring water content and relative saturation. Further, temperature impact on adsorption mechanism is examined for both MO and NEO. The MOFs substantially reduced water content in both oils, and filtration during ageing lowered moisture and slowed degradation relative to the controls. These findings establish MOF filtration as a field-compatible strategy for extending transformer insulation life.
keywords: "Insulation;Mineral oil; Natural ester oil; Dielectric Spectroscopy; BDV; PD; Moisture dynamics"

name: Ameer Suhail
thesis_title: A Scalable Optofluidic Microreactor Platform: Development and Demonstration for Photocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution, Overall Water Splitting, and Liquid-Phase Alkylation
abstract: Photocatalytic water splitting offers a simple route to green hydrogen, but scaling it up requires reactors that couple catalysts effectively to light, water and product removal. Existing flat panels are hydrodynamically passive, while optofluidic microreactors depend on fabrication routes too costly for large areas. This thesis develops a scalable optofluidic microreactor platform on commercial soda-lime glass, using laser-lithography-assisted wet etching and spray-coated catalyst immobilization with a colloidal-silica binder. The route needs no clean room or photomask, and was extended to large-area plates with a favourable projected cost. The platform was demonstrated in three projects. Immobilized Pt–CdS nanowires gave visible-light hydrogen evolution well above a matched suspension reactor. Al-doped SrTiO? achieved overall water splitting without sacrificial reagents in a CFD-guided reactor, with activity strongly governed by flow and bubble removal. A serpentine reactor then performed continuous-flow tert-butylation of phenol, and numbering up plates in parallel increased conversion at unchanged throughput. One fabrication route thus served three different reactions, with the limits in each case traced to identified causes.
keywords: Optofluidic microreactor; Photocatalytic water splitting; Hydrogen evolution; Overall water splitting; Laser-lithography-assisted wet etching; Spray coating; Computational fluid dynamics; tert-Butylation of phenol; Continuous-flow chemistry; Scalable fabrication

name: AMIT KUMAR CHAURASIYA
thesis_title: Deep Learning-Driven Design and Biomechanical Optimization of Patient-Specific PEEK Cranial Implants
abstract: Cranial defects resulting from trauma, tumour resection, or decompressive surgery require implants that restore protection, symmetry, and mechanical integrity. Conventional titanium and PMMA implants are often limited by stress shielding, imaging artefacts, poor patient-specific fit, or insufficient strength. Polyetheretherketone (PEEK), a high-performance, radiolucent polymer with bone-like stiffness, is a promising alternative, particularly when patient-specific implants are produced via additive manufacturing. This research develops an integrated workflow for the design and biomechanical optimization of patient-specific PEEK cranial implants. Computed tomography data are segmented using U-Net-family deep learning models, with Attention U-Net giving the best performance, and the segmented skull is reconstructed into three-dimensional models using Marching Cubes. Implant geometries are then designed to match the patient’s cranial curvature, overcoming the limitations of conventional geometric hole-filling methods. Finite element analysis under physiological and impact loading evaluates stress and deformation, and structural and fixation-location optimization is applied to ensure mechanical adequacy. The structural performance of PEEK is compared with titanium and PMMA to establish its suitability as the primary implant material. Overall, the work aims to provide a systematic, patient-specific, and mechanically validated approach to cranial implant design that supports safer, better-fitting reconstruction and future clinical translation.
keywords: Deep Learning Segmentation; Patient-Specific Implant; Cranioplasty; Medical Image Segmentation; Computed Tomography; Fixation Optimization; Biomechanical Optimization; 3D Reconstruction; Additive manufacturing

name: Amit Kumar Maury
thesis_title: Structural and Magnetic Properties of  Pseudo-1D Spin Chain Compounds
abstract: This research investigates relationships between crystal structure, magnetic interactions, electronic structure, and spin dynamics in low-dimensional, geometrically frustrated materials, particularly Ca3Co2O6, its substituted compound, and NiTe2O5. It combines experimental studies with DFT calculations to understand how chemical substitution modifies magnetic exchange interactions and electronic states. A major focus is the pseudo-one-dimensional spin-chain compound Ca3Co2O6, where competing intra-chain ferromagnetic (J1 > 0) and inter-chain antiferromagnetic (J2 < 0) interactions produce magnetic frustration and complex behaviour. Samples are synthesized by solid-state reaction and sol-gel methods and characterized using X-ray diffraction with Rietveld refinement, Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and magnetic measurements using a Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS). In Er-substituted Ca3-xErxCo2O6, Er3+ substitution induces partial reduction of Co3+ to Co2+ for charge balance, weakening magnetic ordering, suppressing transition temperatures, and reducing field-induced transitions. It also promotes cluster-glass-like behaviour with slow relaxation and Vogel-Fulcher-type freezing. Zr substitution preferentially at trigonal-prismatic sites preserves the one-dimensional chain structure while modifying magnetic interactions and enhancing glassy behaviour. These investigations provide insight into controlling nonequilibrium magnetic states with potential relevance to memory and storage applications. Experimental results and DFT calculations are used together to interpret structural, magnetic, and electronic properties at the microscopic level.
keywords: Low-Dimensional Magnetism; Geometrical Frustration; Magnetic Phase Transitions; Magnetization; Statistical Analysis; Mathematical Modelling; Density Functional Theory; VASP; Quantum espresso; Wien2k; Cluster-Glass Behaviour; Thermal Memory

name: Amit Kumar Sahu
thesis_title: Development and Performance Evaluation of Ready-Mix Thermal Insulation Foam Plaster
abstract: Thermal insulation of building envelopes is critical for reducing operational energy demand, yet conventional cement–sand plasters offer poor insulation, while lightweight aggregate-based thermal plasters remain costly and regionally scarce in India. This doctoral research develops foam concrete (FC) plasters as cost-effective, locally adaptable thermal insulating renders. FC is produced by the mixed foam method using OPC, Class-F fly ash, sodium lauryl sulphate as surfactant, and, where applicable, LECA, silica fume and polypropylene fibres. The influence of water-to-solid ratio and surfactant dosage on air entrainment, stability, strength, hydration phases (XRD), water absorption and thermal conductivity was systematically established. Building on this, foamed plasters of 1000 and 600 kg/m³ density classes were designed and benchmarked against conventional 1:3 and 1:6 mortars. All mixes met EN 998-1 consistency requirements with excellent stability (?1% settlement), achieved 28-day compressive and flexural strengths up to 4.1 and 0.68 MPa, and reduced thermal conductivity from 0.98 to 0.14 W/m·K, an approximate 85% reduction. Ongoing work addresses hygric performance, energy simulation across Indian climatic zones using DesignBuilder, techno-economic and payback analysis, and validation through plastered prototype walls against conventional plaster. This research thus offers a sustainable, cost-effective and practical plastering solution for energy-efficient buildings in Indian construction practice.
keywords: Foam Concrete Plaster; Thermal Insulating Plaster; Mixed Foam Method; Lightweight Cementitious Composites; Thermal Conductivity; Energy-Efficient Buildings

name: AMRITAVA SARKAR
thesis_title: Development of TiTaNbMoW Refractory High Entropy Alloys and Aluminium Matrix Surface Composites
abstract: My research in materials science and metallurgical engineering focuses on solid-state manufacturing, surface engineering, and advanced metallic materials, rigorously correlating processing conditions and microstructural evolution with mechanical, tribological, and corrosion performance. My expertise spans friction stir processing (FSP), mechanical alloying, arc melting, and refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). Key research contributions include: Surface Nanocomposites: Fabricated ZrO2?SiO2 and TiNbMoTaW nanoparticle-reinforced AA5083 surface composites using multi-pass FSP, establishing processing–microstructure–property relationships that dramatically improve surface hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion protection. Refractory High-Entropy Alloys: Synthesized equiatomic TiNbMoTaW RHEAs via mechanical alloying and arc melting, integrating CALPHAD-based thermodynamic modelling to evaluate phase constitution, stability, and high-temperature suitability. Laminated Structures: Characterized Al/Cu laminated structures produced via friction stir additive manufacturing, focusing on interfacial microstructures, intermetallic compound evolution, metallurgical bonding strength, and fracture mechanics. This work advances the fundamental understanding of degradation analysis, tribology, and solid-state joining. Findings have been published in reputable peer-reviewed journals including Advanced Powder Technology, Materials Chemistry and Physics, and Engineering Failure Analysis. For the hybrid ceramic or RHEA system, FSP successfully enhanced surface hardness, superior wear resistance, and improved corrosion performance. My long-term research goal is to develop energy-efficient materials processing and fabrication technologies for advanced engineering and energy applications.

name: Aniket Banerjee
discipline: School of Interdisciplinary Studies and Sustainability
thesis_title: Expansion of the Genetic Code: Development of Fluorescent Triazolyl Unnatural Amino Acids Encoded T7 RNA Polymerase, Superoxide Dismutase A, and ?-Galactosidase, and Generation of Orthogonal Aminoacyl tRNA Synthetase Library
abstract: Dr. Aniket Banerjee is a PhD-trained biotechnology and chemical biology researcher with expertise in protein engineering, genetic code expansion, recombinant protein expression and purification, and biochemical characterisation. His doctoral research at the Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati focused on developing orthogonal aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase/tRNA systems and incorporating fluorescent triazolyl unnatural amino acids into proteins, including superfolder GFP, T7 RNA polymerase, manganese superoxide dismutase and ?-galactosidase. He has hands-on experience in molecular cloning, PCR, site-directed mutagenesis, in-vitro transcription and translation, enzyme activity assays, fluorescence and UV–visible spectroscopy, fluorescence lifetime measurements, MALDI-TOF, LC–MS, circular dichroism and electrophoretic techniques. His broader technical experience includes microbiological assays, cell-based assays, microscopy, nanoparticle characterisation and computational tools such as AutoDock and GROMACS. He has contributed to peer-reviewed publications, a patent application, research grant development and laboratory setup, and has mentored undergraduate, postgraduate and intern researchers. He is interested in applying his experimental, analytical and problem-solving capabilities to research and development in biotechnology, biopharmaceuticals, diagnostics and life-science innovation.

name: ANIL KUMAR SAH
thesis_title: “Experimental Characterization and Multiphysics Modelling of SS420–IN718 Functionally Graded Structures Produced by Dual-Wire Plasma-Based Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing”
abstract: Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) has emerged as a promising technology for fabricating functionally graded materials (FGMs) with tailored microstructural and mechanical properties. This research focuses on the experimental characterization and multiphysics modelling of SS420–IN718 functionally graded structures fabricated using a dual-wire plasma-based WAAM process. The influence of material composition and processing conditions on bead geometry, microstructural evolution, phase formation, mechanical properties, and residual stress development is investigated. Advanced characterization techniques, including optical microscopy, SEM, EDS, EBSD, TEM, and XRD, are employed to examine microstructural features, elemental distribution, crystallographic characteristics, and phase evolution. Mechanical behaviour is evaluated through microhardness and tensile testing, while residual stresses are assessed using the XRD sin²? method. Furthermore, numerical models are developed in COMSOL Multiphysics to investigate transient temperature distributions, thermal cycles, melt pool behaviour, droplet transfer dynamics, and thermally induced residual stresses. The numerical investigations incorporate coupled heat transfer, fluid flow, electromagnetic effects, and solid mechanics to understand the underlying physical mechanisms governing material deposition. The integration of experimental observations and numerical predictions aims to establish process–structure–property relationships and provide insights into the controlled fabrication and improved performance of multi-material functionally graded structures using plasma-based WAAM.
keywords: Plasma-based Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing; Functionally Graded Materials; SS420–IN718; Multiphysics Modelling; Microstructural Characterization; Residual Stress; Droplet Transfer.

name: Anjali Singh
discipline: Department of Humanities and Social Sciences
thesis_title: Drivers of FDI and the effect of FDI on the market structure of the host country
abstract: Foreign firms engage in FDI based on the idea that some firms have special assets that provide them a competitive edge over domestic firms. Literature that estimates the spillover effect of the presence of foreign firms has found inconclusive results due to the under-exploration of the competitive effects. We examine the drivers of FDI and its effects on the host country’s market structure, both theoretically and empirically. Using a generalized oligopoly model and focusing on two policy instruments, taxes and infrastructure, the study investigates the conditions under which firms’ concentration in a country becomes an equilibrium outcome. The next study explores the welfare implications of a foreign firm’s entry, and under what circumstances the deregulation of foreign firm entry should be suggested. Using a vertically related market with an upstream duopoly and a downstream oligopoly, we show that even in the absence of spillovers and direct positive backward linkages, there are conditions under which it would be beneficial to attract foreign firms. We further empirically examine the heterogeneous impact of ownership on market power through price-cost markup and identify the determinants of the foreign ownership markup premium using a firm-level panel dataset of Indian manufacturing industries.
keywords: Industrial organisation; International trade; Development Economics

name: ANKIT
thesis_title: Machine Learning–Accelerated Nonlinear Contact Mechanics: From Geometry-Aware Contact Search to Adhesive Friction Homogenization
abstract:
When surfaces touch, stick, or slide, their interactions influence how machines and materials behave. Simulating these interactions accurately can be computationally expensive. This doctoral research combines finite element methods with scientific machine learning to accelerate contact calculations and describe the behavior of rough, adhesive interfaces.

The completed study focuses on finding the closest point on a surface, a calculation repeated throughout contact simulations. A generative adversarial network incorporates geometric constraints to provide better starting estimates for a conventional numerical solver. In benchmark tests, this hybrid approach reduced calculation time by approximately 20% while preserving the accuracy of the conventional method.

The ongoing study investigates how surface roughness and adhesion affect friction. Computational homogenization translates detailed interactions within a small repeating surface region into an equivalent smooth interface with the same overall response. A predictive model constrained by physics is being developed to estimate effective friction from surface geometry, with the aim of avoiding repeated detailed simulations.

By connecting geometric information with the mechanics of interacting surfaces, this research explores how machine learning can support established simulation methods. The goal is faster, physically consistent predictions that help researchers study contact, friction, and adhesion without resolving every detail of the underlying surface.
keywords: Computational Contact Mechanics; Finite Element Method; Scientific Machine Learning; Generative AI; Deep Learning; Generative Adversarial Networks; Surrogate Modeling; Graph Neural Networks; Physics-Constrained Machine Learning; Computational Homogenization

name: Anterdipan Singh
thesis_title: Optical Modelling, TCAD Simulation, and Experimental Investigation of ITO/n-MoS2-x/p-Si(c)/p+-Si(Al)/Ag heterojunction Solar cells
abstract:
**Abstract**
Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), particularly molybdenum disulfide (MoS???), have emerged as promising materials for next-generation silicon heterojunction solar cells owing to their tunable optoelectronic properties, intrinsic n-type conductivity, and favorable band alignment with silicon. This work presents a comprehensive investigation of defect engineering, optical parameter extraction, and physics-based device modeling of ITO/n-MoS???/p-Si(c)/p?-Si(Al)/Ag heterojunction solar cells. A novel approach is developed to extract the refractive index of ultrathin MoS??? films deposited on non-transparent silicon substrates without relying on optical interference fringes. The experimentally derived optical constants are incorporated into TCAD Sentaurus simulations using the transfer-matrix method to investigate light propagation and absorption. Furthermore, a two-defect electrical model is established to distinguish the contributions of sulfur vacancy-induced donor states and recombination centers. To validate the modeling framework, MoS??? thin films with controlled sulfur vacancy concentrations are synthesized using dual-zone chemical vapor deposition and characterized through XPS, Raman, photoluminescence, and electron microscopy. The experimentally extracted material parameters are subsequently integrated into device simulations, demonstrating strong agreement between simulated and measured photovoltaic characteristics. This work establishes an integrated experimental and computational framework for understanding defect-mediated optoelectronic behavior and optimizing MoS???/Si heterojunction solar cells.
keywords: MoS???; Silicon heterojunction solar cells;  Defect-based TCAD modeling; Optical constants; Refractive index extraction; Dual-zone chemical vapor deposition (DZCVD); Plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD); Thermal evaporation; RF/DC sputtering; Finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulation; Transfer-matrix method (TMM).

name: Anubhab Mukherjee
thesis_title: Seismic Strengthening of Unreinforced Masonry Buildings using Ferrocement Bands
abstract: Unreinforced masonry (URM) buildings are highly vulnerable to earthquakes because of their brittle behavior, low tensile and shear strengths, and inadequate structural integrity. This thesis evaluates ferrocement bands as an economical seismic strengthening technique through integrated experimental and numerical investigations. Following material characterization, three-dimensional nonlinear finite element models were developed and validated in ABAQUS. Six ferrocement mesh–matrix combinations were assessed numerically and through 108 masonry wallette tests under diagonal compression and four-point bending. Gauge 10 welded wire mesh with Renderoc SP40 demonstrated favourable overall performance and was selected for full-scale strengthening. A single-storey URM building strengthened using the Splint and Bandage configuration prescribed in IS 13935 was tested under quasi-static reverse cyclic loading. Strengthening increased lateral capacity approximately 2.4-fold, doubled deformation capacity, enhanced energy absorption 3.5–5.3-fold, and reduced out-of-plane deformation by nearly 97%. The failure response shifted from brittle shear damage to stable rocking, indicating improved box action. Subsequently, 828 validated numerical simulations quantified governing strengthening and structural parameters, identified effective strengthening ranges, and supported development of a regression-based empirical equation for lateral capacity prediction. The findings provide quantitative guidance for practical ferrocement strengthening and seismic assessment of vulnerable URM buildings across component and building scales.
keywords: Unreinforced masonry; URM buildings; Strengthening; Ferrocement bands; Finite element modeling; Lateral load behavior; Wire mesh; Splint and Bandage

name: Anuj Narode
thesis_title: Monogeneity and Arithmetic of Number Fields
abstract:
Understanding when the ring of integers of a number field admits a power integral basis is a central problem in algebraic number theory. This thesis investigates monogeneity through explicit polynomial families and cyclotomic subfields, using Dedekind's criterion, Newton polygons, discriminants, and ramification.

For pure fields defined by $x^{2\cdot3^s\cdot q^r}-m$, with squarefree $m\ne\pm1$ and prime $q\equiv2\pmod3$, we give congruence conditions for the defining root to generate the ring of integers and identify common index divisors forcing non-monogeneity. For $(x^2+1)^n-ax^n$, we compute discriminants and characterize primes dividing the index.

We construct infinite families of monogenic prime-degree polynomials with non-squarefree discriminants, unconditionally in certain ranges and, elsewhere, under the number-field $abc$-conjecture. We also prove non-monogeneity for a family involving Stirling numbers.

For monic irreducible reciprocal polynomials $f(x)=x^n g(x+x^{-1})$, we relate discriminants and indices and prove that $f$ is monogenic precisely when $g$ is monogenic and $f(1)$ and $f(-1)$ are individually squarefree. We obtain conditional infinite families in degrees five and ten, and an unconditional lower bound $\gg N/\log N$ for a sextic family.

Finally, we study Galois groups and monogeneity of cyclotomic subfields, proving that every subfield of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m)$ is monogenic for $m=2^n,3^n$, or $4\cdot3^n$. For $m=2^n,4\cdot3^n$, $\zeta_m-\zeta_m^{-1}$ generates explicit power integral bases.
keywords: Monogeneity, Power integral basis, Galois Groups, cyclotomic fields, Abelian extensions

name: Anusua Das
thesis_title: Developemen of Shear Wave Dispersion Imaging Models for Ultrasound Viscoelastography
abstract: Commercially accessible shear wave imaging systems monitor group shear wave speed (SWS) and typically provide stiffness parameters using pure elastic material models. Soft tissues, however, are viscoelastic, and higher-order material models are necessary to characterize the dispersion associated with broadband shear waves. Biological tissues display frequency-dependent nonlinear dispersion in shear wave dispersion imaging. The dispersive behaviour is due to the viscosity of soft tissues and may be correlated with tissue pathology. This research work reviews different techniques to measure phase velocity and dispersion slope. Deep learning models are also developed to estimate shear wave dispersion as well as to reconstruct shear wave dispersion maps from spatio-temporal velocity field data . The results demonstrate the potential of deep learning for efficient shear wave dispersion imaging and quantitative characterization of tissue viscoelasticity. The study suggests that shear wave dispersion imaging can be a valuable technique alongside shear wave elastography in tissue characterisation and disease diagnosis.
keywords: Biomedical Signal Processing; Ultrasound Shear Wave Imaging; Medical Image Reconstruction; Machine  Learning and Deep Learning for Signal Processing.

name: Arindam Maity
thesis_title: Robust Portfolio Optimization with Intractable Claims, Drift Ambiguity, and Model Uncertainty: Investment, Insurance, and Pension Applications
abstract:
The financial market is extremely volatile, and, beyond intrinsic factors, asset performance is influenced by geopolitical conflicts, institutional failures, or economic disruptions. Further, investors face external payoffs arising from non-financial setups that can affect their wealth. Anticipating these external claims, accurately estimating statistical parameters, or identifying the underlying probability measure is very challenging. Failure to correctly identify these factors creates sources of ambiguity.

The thesis investigates robust portfolio optimization problems across individual and institutional frameworks, including insurance and pension fund settings. We incorporate three sources of uncertainty: dependence ambiguity associated with non-hedgeable payoffs, drift ambiguity, and model uncertainty concerning the underlying probability measure. 

Under these ambiguous financial environments, the thesis explores how external non-hedgeable payoffs, individual behavioral biases, and underlying market dynamics influence investment decisions and portfolio outcomes across different financial settings. Specifically, we develop wealth or growth-rate maximization problems under investment objectives such as wealth management, target-driven investing, benchmark-relative performance with different risk measures, and utility preferences, including mean-variance, mean-semivariance, and S-shaped utility, incorporating relevant constraints.

The thesis extends robust portfolio optimization frameworks to diverse financial problems and develops robust investment strategies under different sources of ambiguity, investor objectives, and risk preferences.
keywords: Robust Portfolio Optimization; Portfolio Management; Investment-Insurance Optimization; Pension Fund Management; Stochastic Control; Quantile Formulation

name: ARITRA RAY
thesis_title: Spin-dependent magnetic and thermoelectric phenomena in thin films for spintronic and  spin-caloritronic applications

name: Arpita Deb Singha
thesis_title: Spin-Dynamics in Geometrically-Frustrated Kagomé Planes of Cobalt-Spinels

name: Arunima Dhar
discipline: School of Agro and Rural Technology
thesis_title: A study on Anti-Inflammatory properties of some selected Citrus products
abstract: Chronic inflammation underlies many diseases, and food-based alternatives to anti-inflammatory drugs are increasingly sought. This work examined four citrus fruits (Citrus maxima, C. macroptera, C. limon, C. reticulata) and their products. Sixteen products in 64 variations were prepared, and ten were selected by sensory acceptability. Pectin, uronic acid, vitamin C, folate and phytochemicals were quantified. C. macroptera and its pulp-infused herbal chew performed best. In LPS-stimulated Caco-2 cells, polysaccharide extracts and digested fractions reduced TNF-?, IL-6, IL-8 and COX-2 expression. Peel and pulp showed the highest activity in BSA denaturation, protease inhibition and nitric oxide scavenging assays. The optimized herbal chew retained high levels of vitamin C and uronic acid, was sensorially acceptable, and showed the highest in vitro anti-inflammatory activity of all products tested. A randomized human clinical trial then evaluated the chew’s effect on inflammatory biomarkers (TNF-?, IL-6, CRP), gut-health indicators and safety. The findings support its use as a functional food. Public health prospects were also explored: an affordable, locally sourced product from an underutilized fruit and its peel waste could help manage diet-related inflammation, add value to regional agriculture and reduce food waste.
keywords: Citrus macroptera; Anti-inflammatory activity; Pectin; Vitamin C; Herbal chew; Caco-2 cells; Randomized clinical trial; Public health nutrition

name: Ashirbad Mallick
thesis_title: Development of Ab Initio Collision Models for Direct Simulation Monte Carlo Simulations of Hypersonic Flows
abstract: Developing accurate and computationally efficient models of molecular collisions is essential for predicting high-temperature hypersonic flows, where conventional approaches often struggle to capture thermochemical nonequilibrium. This research bridges first-principles molecular physics and engineering-scale simulations through the development of advanced collision models for Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC). Using ab initio potential energy surfaces and Quasi-Classical Trajectory (QCT) calculations, molecular collision data are incorporated into two novel models: Variable Hard Sphere with Vibrational Favouring (VHSV) and Variable Soft Sphere with Vibrational Favouring (VSSV). These models account for vibrational-state-dependent collision behaviour and anisotropic scattering, providing a more physically representative description of intermolecular interactions. The models are implemented in an in-house DSMC solver and evaluated through transport-property predictions and simulations of canonical flow configurations, including Couette flow and hypersonic flow over a circular cylinder. Their performance is assessed against conventional collision models and established reference data. This work advances the integration of quantum-informed molecular collision physics into high-fidelity computational simulations, offering improved modelling capabilities for rarefied hypersonic flows, atmospheric re-entry, and aerospace thermal protection applications.
keywords: Rarefied Gas Dyamics; Hypersonic flows; DSMC; Molecular Dynamics; Ab initio modelling

name: Ashish Chouhan
discipline: Department of Humanities and Social Sciences
thesis_title: Climate Variablity, Crop insurance and Farmers' Welfare in Madhya Pradesh
abstract: Climate variability poses a serious risk to agricultural production and farm incomes in India, particularly in rainfed regions. This study examines how climate variability affects crop yields in Madhya Pradesh and how far crop insurance under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) protects farmers against this risk. District panel estimates for 1982–2017 show that positive temperature anomalies reduce maize and soybean yields, while negative rainfall anomalies reduce soybean, maize and rice yields, with the largest losses at lower yield quantiles. Although nominal protection per hectare has increased, its real value has declined since 2018–19, more sharply in Madhya Pradesh than nationally, alongside falling coverage and limited participation of non-loanee farmers. Double-hurdle estimates for 395 soybean farmers in Ujjain and Betul show that age, education, farm size and access to credit raise the likelihood of adoption, while Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe farmers are less likely to insure. Conditional on adoption, leasing-in land and crop diversification are associated with lower coverage. Endogenous switching regression indicates that insurance raises farm income and per capita consumption, with substantial potential gains for non-adopters. Crop insurance improves farmers’ welfare, but eroding real protection and unequal participation weaken its role in managing climate risk.
keywords: Climate variability; Crop yields; Crop insurance; PMFBY; Farmers’ welfare

name: Ashish Kumar
thesis_title: Design of Sub-THz On-Chip Filters for Next Generation Wireless Communication Networks
abstract:
My doctoral research at the Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati focuses on the design and development of compact, high-performance RF, millimeter-wave (mm-wave), and sub-terahertz (sub-THz) passive circuits for next-generation wireless communication systems, particularly 6G and beyond-5G applications.

A major research area involves the design of on-chip bandpass filters (BPFs) around 280 GHz using 130 nm SiGe BiCMOS technology, incorporating Spoof Surface Plasmon Polaritons (SSPP), Substrate Integrated Waveguide (SIW), plasmonic waveguides, resonator loading, and fractal structures. The work includes electromagnetic modelling, circuit analysis, optimization, Cadence Virtuoso-based RFIC layout, and semiconductor tape-out preparation through the IHP process.

Additionally, I have developed compact SSPP–SIW hybrid BPFs for Ka-band, V-band, and mm-wave applications, employing transition-free configurations, resonator loading, and Defected Ground Structures (DGS) to improve selectivity, impedance matching, stopband suppression, and miniaturization. My ongoing research explores multiband, dual-band, and frequency-reconfigurable filter architectures.

I have hands-on experience with CST Studio Suite, Ansys HFSS, Lumerical FDTD/MODE, Keysight ADS, COMSOL Multiphysics, and Cadence Virtuoso. My expertise also covers RF prototype fabrication, micromachining, LPKF ProtoLaser U4-based laser fabrication, VNA calibration, and two-port S-parameter measurements (S11/S21) for experimental validation.

Overall, my research integrates RF/microwave engineering, semiconductor technology, RFIC design, electromagnetic simulation, fabrication, and experimental characterization to develop compact, highly selective passive components for future mm-wave and sub-THz communication systems.
keywords: On chip; Bandpass filter; Sub Terahertz; CST; ADS; Cadence virtuoso; Millimeter wave; Spoof surface plasmon polaritons; substrate-integrated waveguide; 130 nm SiGe BiCMOS technology

name: ASHUTOSH SINGH
discipline: School of Interdisciplinary Studies and Sustainability
thesis_title: Ozonation-Based Advanced Degradation of Phenolic and Refractory Pollutants in Refinery Wastewater
abstract:
Petroleum refinery wastewater contains complex and refractory pollutants, including phenolic compounds, oil, ammonia, and other organic contaminants, which are difficult to remove through conventional treatment methods. This research investigates ozone-based Advanced Oxidation Processes (AOPs), including ozonation, catalytic ozonation, peroxone (O?/H?O?), and catalytic peroxone (O?/H?O?/ZnFe?O?), for effective wastewater treatment.

Initially, 4-nitrophenol (4NP) degradation was investigated in an ozone bubble column reactor. At pH 11 and an ozone feed rate of 0.50 mg s?¹, 4NP concentration decreased below the detection limit within 5 minutes. ZnO-assisted catalytic ozonation further enhanced degradation efficiency under alkaline conditions.

The peroxone process achieved up to 97.3% phenol removal, 98% ammonia removal, 98.5% colour removal, and 98% COD removal from petroleum refinery wastewater. Additionally, ZnFe?O?-assisted catalytic peroxone achieved 99% degradation of 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) within 5 minutes, along with 64% total organic carbon (TOC) removal. Treatment of DNP-spiked refinery wastewater resulted in 81% DNP degradation, 98% COD removal, and 96% oil removal.

Overall, the findings demonstrate that ozone-based hybrid oxidation processes offer promising solutions for rapid pollutant degradation and efficient treatment of complex industrial wastewater, with performance influenced by pH, oxidant dosage, and catalyst selection.
keywords: Petroleum Refinery Wastewater; Advanced Oxidation Processes; Catalytic Ozonation; Peroxone Process; Nitrophenolic Pollutants; Degradation Kinetics.

name: Bhoomika Patel
thesis_title: Lovastatin production by A.terreus under submerged fermentation
abstract: The Indian statin market is expanding owing to the increasing prevalence of cardiovascular disease. IMARC Group anticipates Indian market to attain USD 677 million by 2034, with a compound annual growth of 2.66% from 2026 to 2034.  Lovastatin, a secondary metabolite produced by Aspergillus terreus, has gained interest for its cholesterol-lowering effects. Biosynthesis of lovastatin through fermentation is constrained by intricate interrelationships with fungal morphology. Current research systematically navigated through these challenges to increase lovastatin production. In the first stage, fungal pellet morphology was tweaked by incorporating organic source in fermentation media. In the subsequent phase, Plackett-Burman screening of media components and central composite design (CCD) to estimate mutual interaction with a goal of increasing lovastatin titer. Continuous improvement in productivity is essential for the success of a fermentation process. However, success of batch mode is restricted due to substrate depletion. As an alternative, a fed-batch strategy was employed wherein substrate feeding strategies was optimized ensuring continuous supply of substrate which in turn supported better lovastatin productivity. Next, we investigated the application of lovastatin as a potential anti-cancer agent. Preliminary in vitro MTT, colony and migration assay was performed. Molecular docking studies provided computational validation of its potential anticancer activity.
keywords: Fungal fermentation; Lovastatin; Upstream and downstream processing; Solvent extraction;HPLC; Design Expert;Secondary Metabolite; Fed Batch

name: Bhushan Ballav Pathak
thesis_title: Spoof Surface Plasmon Polariton based Flexible Microwave Filters for Radio Stripe Network Applications
abstract: The rapid evolution of Beyond Fifth Generation (B5G) and Sixth Generation (6G) wireless systems is driving the need for compact, low-loss, flexible, and highly integrated radio-frequency (RF) components. This thesis investigates Spoof Surface Plasmon Polaritons (SSPP)-based microwave filters for emerging distributed wireless architectures, including Radio Stripe Networks. A range of compact, uniplanar, and flexible SSPP filters are proposed, designed, fabricated, and experimentally characterized. The designs employ engineered periodic unit cells, including novel geometries, interdigital loading, folded structures, and higher-order modes, to tailor dispersion characteristics and achieve miniaturization, wide or multiband operation, and improved electromagnetic confinement. Dual-band configurations are explored through modal interaction and overlapped periodic structures. The proposed filters demonstrate low insertion loss, effective stopband suppression, and stable operation under bending and conformal conditions. Equivalent circuit models are developed to explain the operating mechanisms and provide physical insight, with predictions validated against full-wave simulations and measurements. Fabricated prototypes on ultra-thin flexible polyimide substrates are evaluated experimentally to assess RF performance and mechanical robustness. Overall, this work advances the design and understanding of flexible SSPP-based microwave filtering structures and establishes their potential for compact, conformal RF front ends in next-generation wireless communication systems.
keywords: Spoof Surface Plasmon Polariton (SSPP) ; Microwave Filters; Radio stripe networks (RSNs); Flexible filters; Equivalent circuit modelling of SSPP; RF and Microwave Engineering

name: Bibek Goswami
thesis_title: Early Diagnosis of Oral Cancer Using Multiple Imaging Modalities: Trustworthy and Efficient Deep Learning from White-Light Photographs, CT and Histopathology Images
abstract: Oral cancer is often diagnosed at an advanced stage, when treatment is more difficult and survival is lower. Subjective examinations, limited access to specialists, and time-consuming manual planning can contribute to delays. This thesis investigates three imaging modalities across the care pathway. For screening, white-light photographs are represented using color and texture features from multiple color spaces and classified with LightGBM, achieving 99.25% accuracy in binary classification and 98.88% in lesion staging. TrustNet localizes lesions in full photographs and incorporates patient-level evaluation, uncertainty estimation, and calibration, reducing calibration error from 0.278 to 0.036. A history-guided cascade further limits unnecessary image inference on smartphones. For treatment planning, three compact 3D networks, RCGA-Net, MSCBAG-Net, and BRIDGE-Net, segment organs at risk in head-and-neck CT, with overall Dice scores of 0.89–0.93 on PDDCA and HaN-Seg. BRIDGE-Net has approximately 0.10 million parameters and was evaluated on edge hardware. For diagnostic confirmation, AIRNet uses iterative self-refinement to segment tumor regions in histopathology, achieving a Dice score of 0.907. Across the pathway, each method addresses modality-specific challenges and is assessed using class-sensitive metrics, statistical analysis, and computational-cost reporting. The results indicate that compact models can support tasks spanning screening, treatment planning, and confirmation.
keywords: Medical Image Segmentation; Deep Learning; Computer Vision; Large Language Models; Multimodal Learning; LLM Evaluation; Lightweight Neural Networks; Attention Mechanisms; Vision Transformers; Gradient Boosting; Cancer Image Classification; Edge Deployment; Model Training and Evaluation; Machine Learning

name: Bichkar Onkar Vijay
thesis_title: Study on bubble dynamics in Newtonian and viscoelastic surrounding media
abstract:
I am a PhD researcher in Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) with expertise in fluid mechanics, multiphase flows, and Newtonian and viscoelastic fluid dynamics. My doctoral research at the Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati focuses on complex bubble dynamics, including toroidal bubble shrinkage, deformation and breakup of rising bubbles, and the influence of temperature variations on bubble behaviour in viscoelastic fluids.
My research involves numerical modelling and simulation of transient two-phase flows using Basilisk, an open-source CFD framework. I also have experience working with ANSYS Fluent for CFD simulations and engineering flow analysis. My technical expertise includes multiphase flow modelling, numerical methods, computational modelling, simulation analysis, and post-processing and visualization of complex flow fields using ParaView and Tecplot.
Beyond my doctoral research, I have explored the application of CFD to engineering problems, including battery thermal management using phase change materials (PCM). My research experience has strengthened my understanding of fluid mechanics, numerical modelling, heat transfer, and the interpretation of complex physical phenomena.
I am interested in applying my computational and analytical skills to industrial R&D, CFD engineering, thermal-fluid systems, and simulation-driven product development, contributing to the development and optimization of engineering solutions.
keywords: Computational fluid dynamics; Multiphase flows; Numerical modeling; Newtonian and viscoelastic fluid; Heat transfer

name: Biswajit Bhattacharjya
thesis_title: Magnetic Photocatalysts in Wastewater Treatment and its Recovery
abstract: The presence of pharmaceutically active compounds (PhACs) in aquatic environments has emerged as a significant environmental concern, necessitating the development of efficient and sustainable wastewater treatment technologies. Among various approaches, photocatalysis has attracted considerable attention; however, limited visible-light utilization, rapid charge-carrier recombination, and difficulties in catalyst recovery remain major challenges. Magnetic photocatalysts offer the advantage of facile separation and recovery using an external magnetic field, thereby minimizing secondary contamination. In this context, the proposed research aims to develop bioinspired magnetic photocatalysts, including Fe3O4, NiO, and Co3O4, using Mimosa pudica and Camellia sinensis extracts as natural reducing and stabilizing agents. Preliminary investigations demonstrated the successful synthesis of Mimosa pudica-mediated Fe3O4 nanoparticles with an average crystallite size of 28.30 nm, saturation magnetization of 74.77 emu/g, and a reduced optical bandgap of 1.48 eV. The material achieved 87.75% ciprofloxacin degradation under visible-light irradiation and 87.5% magnetic recovery after five reuse cycles. Building on these findings, the study will investigate transition metal and gadolinium doping, Fe3O4/NiO/Co3O4 heterostructure development, and photocatalytic performance under visible irradiation. Furthermore, laboratory and pilot-scale experiments, followed by continuous-flow reactor development, will be undertaken to establish an efficient and recoverable wastewater treatment system.
keywords: Pharmaceutical Active Compounds; Bio-based magnetic photocatalysts; Catalyst recovery; Ecotoxicity analysis

name: Biswajit Das
thesis_title: Word Representations of Graphs: Repetition Patterns and Structural Properties
abstract:
We study word-representable graphs, focusing on repetition avoidance, generalised representations, formal languages, and graph structure.

We solve an open problem proposed by Kitaev and Lozin in Words and Graphs: every word-representable graph, except the empty graph on two vertices, admits a non-trivial square-free representation. We count square-free representations of complete graphs, identify a non-complete graph with finitely many square-free representations, and prove that other non-complete connected word-representable graphs admit infinitely many. We introduce p-complete squares, characterise them for small p, and prove that every K_p-free circle graph admits a p-complete square-free uniform representation. Deciding whether a graph admits a p-complete square-free representation is NP-hard for fixed p.

For 1-11-representations, we establish an equivalence between uniform and multi-interval representations. We show that cubes may be unavoidable in minimum-length representations, while optimal permutational representations are cube-free. We prove that the languages of representations and permutational representations of a fixed graph are regular.

For co-bipartite graphs, we establish vertex-ordering characterisation and give an algorithm constructing 3-uniform representations. We prove that permutation graphs are precisely those with representation number two. Their speed is asymptotically smaller than that of all co-bipartite graphs, and their entropy is zero. We identify bipartite families with word-representable complements.
keywords: Word-representable graphs; 1-11-representable graphs; representation number; square-free; p-complete squre-free; cube-free; regular language; k-multi-interval representation; co-bipartite graphs; complement operation; speed; entropy

name: Bivakar Bose
thesis_title: Some Problems in Stochastic Games
abstract:
My research focuses on Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and stochastic control, which provide mathematical frameworks for making optimal decisions in systems evolving under uncertainty. In an MDP, a controller selects actions based on the current state of a system to minimize expected costs or maximize rewards over time. When multiple decision-makers interact, the problem becomes a stochastic game, where players may have competing or independent objectives. These frameworks have applications in communication networks, queueing systems, epidemiology ,finance etc.

My doctoral research investigates stochastic games in discrete and continuous time under various cost and risk criteria. It includes nonzero-sum discrete-time games involving first-passage discounted costs, zero-sum semi-Markov stopping games under risk-sensitive discounted costs, and partially observable semi-Markov games under first-passage risk probability criteria. A particular focus is on systems with general sojourn-time distributions, stopping decisions and incomplete state information.

The central objective of my work is to develop rigorous mathematical results establishing game values, saddle-point equilibria in zero-sum games, and Nash equilibria in nonzero-sum games, along with the existence and characterization of optimal strategies.
keywords: Markov Decision Processes; Stochastic Games; Stopping Games; Semi-Markov Process; Nash Equilibrium; Partially Observable Games

name: Chiradip Barua
thesis_title: Integrating Field Sensing, Foundation Models and GeoAI for Sustainable Water Management in Tea Plantations of Assam
abstract: Tea is central to the economy of Assam, yet plantations are increasingly exposed to water stress as monsoon rainfall becomes more erratic and dry spells lengthen during critical growth periods. Irrigation in most gardens is scheduled from experience rather than measured soil-water status. This thesis develops an integrated framework for sustainable water management in tea plantations that links field sensing with artificial intelligence across scales. At the field scale, a monitoring setup in a tea garden of Assam records root-zone soil matric potential and moisture with meteorological variables and irrigation events. Explainable machine learning identifies the factors that control root-zone recovery after irrigation and rainfall, and time-series foundation models are benchmarked against conventional approaches to forecast matric potential and give early warning of water stress. At the landscape scale, geospatial foundation models (GeoAI) are adapted to multi-temporal satellite imagery to map tea plantations and monitor crop condition and water stress beyond instrumented sites. A flexible pH sensor is developed for real-time plant health monitoring. Together, these contributions connect point measurements with regional observation, support climate-resilient irrigation scheduling and offer a transferable decision-support approach for plantation crops in monsoon-influenced regions.
keywords: Geospatial Foundation Models; GeoAI; Tea Plantation; Soil Matric Potential; Time-Series Forecasting; Explainable Machine Learning; Remote Sensing; Irrigation Management

name: Cilaveni Satish Chandra
thesis_title: Unified Small-Signal Modeling and Stability Analysis of a Current-Mode Controlled Three-Level Bidirectional Flying Capacitor Converter
abstract: Converters with flying capacitor (FC) suffer from balancing issues and coupling between the FC voltage balancing loop and the main control loop of the converter. Also, the stability of the system is challenging to determine, because of the coupling between these two loops. Hence, this work develops a unified continuous-time small-signal model (SSM) of a current-mode controlled three-level bidirectional FC converter (3-L BFCC) considering the coupling. The derived unified SSM is validated in both simulation and experiment using the Bode plots. Thereafter, the FC voltage balancing loop and the 3-L BFCC stability boundaries are determined using the proposed framework to maintain the FC voltage using active voltage balancing. The derived unified continuous-time SSM is used to determine the FC voltage balancing and the main control loop controller parameters in the frequency domain, considering the loop delays. A lab-scale prototype of the 3-L BFCC is developed to validate the studies, and extensive hardware results are presented in boost and buck configurations of the 3-L BFCC in steady-state and transient conditions.
keywords: Active voltage balancing; bidirectional operation; current-mode control; stability analysis; unified small-signal model

name: Deep Arya
discipline: School of Interdisciplinary Studies and Sustainability
thesis_title: Design and Development of a Digital Inline Holographic System for Underwater Imaging of Microorganisms and Microparticles
abstract: A compact, portable, and cost-effective lensless digital inline holographic microscopy (LDIHM) system was developed to evaluate aquatic health by in situ identifying and kinematically tracking marine and freshwater microplankton. This system addresses the limitations of conventional white-light microscopy, which requires sample collection that alters microorganism morphology and physicochemical properties, introducing measurement errors. Capable of 24-hour autonomous underwater operation, the robust instrument enables stable edge-sensor logging and kinematic analysis during lake deployments. The hardware architecture features a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B that controls an imaging sensor and a laser diode source. This laser is driven by a LM317T constant-current circuit, optimized for voltage drops and heat generation. The mechanical enclosure, designed using SolidWorks, was fabricated from polyvinyl chloride, laser-cut acrylic, and 3D-printed polylactic acid and polyethylene terephthalate glycol. Holographic data is acquired in situ, followed by ex situ signal processing that integrates conventional numerical diffraction algorithms with the FISTA optimization framework to achieve highly focused, noise-free 3D reconstructions. Furthermore, deep learning algorithms utilizing custom loss functions were developed in Python, MATLAB, and TensorFlow to solve inverse computational problems, achieving automated focusing and twin-image suppression for volumetric imaging.
keywords: Lensless Digital Inline Holographic Microscopy; Computational Imaging; Deep Learning; Signal Processing; Embedded Systems; Hardware Prototyping; Autonomous Systems; Inverse Problems; Volumetric Imaging; Optomechanical Design; Instrumentation

name: Deepak Kumar Rathour
thesis_title: Experimental Studies on Vortex-Induced Vibration of Different Bluff Bodies
abstract: An experimental investigation was conducted to examine vortex-induced vibrations (VIV) and wake dynamics of rigidly connected circular and thin elliptical cylinders in a recirculating water channel. The effects of cylinder arrangement, orientation, centre-to-centre spacing, and cross-sectional aspect ratio on vibration response and vortex formation were investigated. For circular cylinders, side-by-side and tandem configurations were examined under low mass-damping conditions. The results showed that cylinder arrangement strongly influences vibration amplitude. Zero-gap side-by-side cylinders exhibited a peak amplitude of 3.20, approximately 4.51 times that of a single cylinder, whereas the tandem configuration suppressed vibration. Varying cylinder spacing produced significant changes in vibration response and wake interference, including merged vortex streets, coherent gap vortices, and independent vortex shedding. For thin elliptical cylinders with aspect ratios ranging from 0.250 to 0.500, a high-amplitude hyper branch was observed at aspect ratios of 0.350 and below, while higher aspect ratios exhibited conventional three-branch responses. Peak amplitudes decreased with increasing aspect ratio, and hysteresis occurred in transition regions. Overall, the findings demonstrate the significant influence of cylinder geometry, arrangement, and spacing on VIV characteristics and wake dynamics, with implications for closely spaced cylindrical structures such as bundled pipelines, piggyback risers, and twin tunnels.
keywords: Vortex-Induced Vibration (VIV); Fluid-Structure Interaction; Rigidly Connected Cylinders; Circular Cylinders; Elliptical Cylinders; Cylinder Arrangement; Gap-Flow Interference; Wake Dynamics; Vortex Shedding; Vibration Amplitude; Synchronisation; Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV)

name: Devendra Kumar
thesis_title: Multifunctional grid connected converter using model predictive control
abstract: The rapid integration of renewable energy resources (RESs) and electric vehicle (EV) charging stations is transforming distribution grids, requiring advanced power electronic converters and control strategies to maintain voltage and current quality within grid-code limits. To address these challenges, unified power quality conditioners (UPQCs) are utilized to form meshed hybrid microgrids by extending the UPQC DC link into a low-voltage DC (LVDC) line parallel to existing AC lines. This configuration enhances power management, accommodates new DC loads, and ensures reliable operation during grid voltage sags. Additionally, dynamic voltage control maximizes the utilization of the UPQC’s series converter to maintain grid-code voltage profiles under extreme load and generation conditions. For energy storage and EV charging applications, finite control set model predictive control (FCS-MPC) is applied to bi-directional DC-DC converters to regulate DC bus voltage and manage battery charging via constant current (CC) and constant voltage (CV) modes. Finally, FCS-MPC is further leveraged in isolated three-phase four-wire grid-forming converters to supply balanced, unbalanced, and non-linear loads via a single voltage-regulation loop, as well as in droop-controlled solar PV-battery hybrid systems to dynamically regulate DC bus voltage based on battery state of charge (SoC) and load variations.
keywords: Battery energy storage system; bi-directional DC-DC converter; electric vehicle (EV) charging; finite control set model predictive control; grid-forming converter; power quality; renewable energy resources (RESs); unified power quality conditioner (UPQC).
