name: Dharanikota Naga Phani Sai Kumar
thesis_title: Design and Synthesis of Novel Amide-Linked Covalent Organic Frameworks and Their Composites for CO2 Capture and Photocatalytic Conversion
abstract: To address climate change and mitigate greenhouse gas emissions, the development of advanced materials for CO2 capture and utilization has become increasingly important. Research focuses on the design, synthesis, structural elucidation, and application of novel amide-linked Covalent Organic Frameworks (COFs) and their composites for CO2 capture and photocatalytic conversion. Novel amide-based COFs and their composites have been successfully synthesized. Their gas adsorption performance was evaluated for CO2, N2, and CH4 under varying temperatures and pressures to understand their adsorption behaviour and separation potential. Ideal Adsorbed Solution Theory (IAST) was employed to estimate the adsorption selectivity of relevant gas mixtures, particularly CO2/N2 and CO2/CH4. Furthermore, the photocatalytic reduction of CO2 using the synthesized COFs has been investigated, evaluating their potential for solar-driven conversion into value-added products. For structural modelling and elucidation, plausible molecular and crystalline structures were constructed using Material Studio. Structural arrangements were simulated, and theoretical predictions were compared with experimental characterization results. My research integrates materials synthesis, computational modelling, physicochemical characterization, gas adsorption analysis, and photocatalysis. Through this work, I have developed practical expertise in porous functional materials, gas separation, and photocatalytic CO2 conversion, contributing to the development of advanced materials for carbon capture, utilization.

name: Dhriti Biswas
discipline: Department of Humanities and Social Sciences
thesis_title: International Spillovers of U.S. Monetary Policy: Transmission, Connectedness, and Policy Autonomy
abstract:
The international transmission of U.S. monetary policy has important implications for global macroeconomic stability, financial interconnectedness, and domestic policy autonomy. The present study examines the heterogeneous effects of U.S. monetary policy shocks across advanced and emerging market economies, emphasising macroeconomic adjustments, financial spillovers, and domestic policy responses.

The analysis addresses three interrelated dimensions of international monetary transmission. First, it investigates the dynamic responses of output, inflation, interest rates, and exchange rates to U.S. monetary policy shocks, assessing heterogeneity across distinct monetary tightening episodes. Second, it evaluates the magnitude, direction, and asymmetry of cross-country financial connectedness, including the potential intermediary role of advanced economies in transmitting shocks to emerging markets. Third, it examines the extent of domestic monetary policy autonomy and assesses whether macroprudential measures mitigate exposure to external monetary disturbances.

The empirical framework combines local projections, vector autoregressive models, and connectedness measures to characterise dynamic responses, cross-market interdependencies, and asymmetric spillover patterns. By integrating broad perspectives, the study seeks to advance understanding of the channels and conditional nature of international monetary transmission, while providing policy relevant evidence on the challenges confronting economies exposed to global monetary shocks.
keywords: U.S. Monetary Policy; International Spillovers; Financial Connectedness Network; Vector Autoregression; Local Projections Modelling.

name: Digvijay Kumar Gupta
discipline: School of Agro and Rural Technology
thesis_title: Integrated Modelling and Performance Assessment of Hydrogen Compression, Grid-Connected Salt Cavern Storage, and Geological Storage Potential in India
abstract:
Integrating renewable energy into India's power grid requires efficient, large-scale energy storage solutions to reduce curtailment and manage surplus electricity. This research investigates the technical feasibility and performance of underground hydrogen storage (UHS) in salt caverns through an integrated thermodynamic, grid-level, and geospatial assessment.
First, a novel liquid-piston compression system coupled with isobaric hydrogen storage is developed and evaluated using energy and exergy analyses to assess compression efficiency and thermodynamic losses. Second, a grid-connected hydrogen storage framework is investigated to quantify storage requirements and evaluate the potential for renewable energy curtailment mitigation and surplus utilization in India's power system. Third, a GIS-based geological suitability assessment of the Nagaur–Ganganagar Basin, Rajasthan, is conducted using halite depth, thickness, and spatial characteristics to identify prospective salt cavern locations and estimate hydrogen storage potential. Finally, comparative thermodynamic analyses of isobaric (volume-compensated) and isochoric (constant-volume) cavern storage configurations are performed to evaluate their operational characteristics, energy requirements, and exergy performance.
The research aims to establish an integrated framework linking efficient hydrogen compression, renewable energy integration, geological storage potential, and cavern operational performance to support the development of large-scale underground hydrogen storage infrastructure in India.

name: Dr. Atul Kumar Gautam
thesis_title: Modeling, Analysis, and Quantitative Identification of Interactive Fault Parameters in a Misaligned-Bowed-Coupled Rotor Train System Integrated with Active Magnetic Bearing
abstract:
Interacting faults in rotating machinery amplify vibration, accelerate wear, and complicate diagnosis. This study develops methods to model, control, and identify simultaneous angular coupling misalignment, residual shaft bow, unbalance, and internal damping in coupled rotor trains. Misalignment modifies coupling stiffness and introduces additive dynamic coupling stiffness. Its interaction with shaft bow generates multiplicative excitation that amplifies vibration and alters harmonic signatures.

Energy-based equations for a two-rotor train are solved in MATLAB/Simulink. Time histories, orbits, and full spectra show that a PID-controlled active magnetic bearing (AMB) reduces vibration and stabilizes orbits. An offset-disc model captures gyroscopic coupling between translation and rotation. Condensing the rotational coordinates enables identification from measured translations. Frequency-domain least squares simultaneously estimates viscous and internal damping, unbalance, bow, static and additive dynamic coupling stiffnesses, multiplicative loads, and AMB displacement and current stiffnesses under measurement noise and modeling uncertainty.

Rig tests use shim-induced misalignment, coupling looseness, and proximity probes. Measured fundamental frequencies, harmonic amplitudes, orbits, and full spectra agree with predictions. A multidisc Timoshenko beam finite-element model incorporates shear deformation, rotary inertia, gyroscopic effects, bearing dynamics, AMB actuation, and interacting excitations. This framework extends fault identification to flexible rotor trains and supports vibration-based diagnosis and condition monitoring.
keywords: Coupled rotor system; vibration analysis and control; Fault analysis and identification; Finite element method; active magnetic bearing; experimental research

name: Evenmore Mylliem
thesis_title: Experimental and Numerical Investigations of Laser Processing of Natural and Synthetic Fabrics
abstract: A doctoral researcher in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati, working under the guidance of Prof. S. N. Joshi. Prior to his PhD, he completed his M.Tech in Mechanical Engineering (Design and Manufacturing) from NIT Silchar in 2019, his B.Tech in Mechanical Engineering from The ICFAI University, Tripura in 2015, and worked as a Trainee Engineer at NIT Meghalaya. name: G SREEKANTH YADAV
thesis_title: Simultaneous Neutralization and Heavy Metal Removal from Secondary Lead Smelting Plant Wastewater and Acid Mine Drainage Using a Mixed Microbial Culture
abstract:
My PhD research focused on developing a biological treatment process using a mixed microbial culture for the simultaneous neutralization, sulfate reduction and heavy-metal removal from acidic industrial wastewater, particularly secondary lead smelting plant (SLSP) wastewater and coal acid mine drainage (AMD). The research involved developing and optimizing a sulfidogenic semi-batch reactor (SmBR), evaluating its performance under different operating conditions, and investigating its applicability to synthetic and actual industrial wastewater containing high sulfate concentrations, acidity and heavy metals.

The research also examined the environmental stability of treatment-generated biosludge through metal leaching studies, chemical speciation and metal mobility assessments under oxic and anoxic conditions. Ecological and human health risk assessments were conducted to evaluate potential risks associated with sludge disposal and exposure. Overall, the findings demonstrate the potential of biological treatment for managing complex acidic industrial wastewater while addressing heavy-metal contamination and associated sludge management challenges.

name: GAURAV PRAKASH
thesis_title: Processing–Structure–Property Relationships in Direct Ink Writing of Alumina Ceramics
abstract: Direct ink writing (DIW) is a promising additive manufacturing technique for fabricating complex ceramic components. However, achieving desirable rheological behaviour, dimensional stability, densification and mechanical performance remains challenging. The present research investigates the processing, rheology and mechanical properties of DIW-fabricated alumina (Al?O?) ceramics, with particular emphasis on particle-size distribution and vacuum-assisted colloidal silica infiltration. Alumina-based inks are formulated and characterized to evaluate their rheological behaviour, including viscosity, yield stress, viscoelastic properties and structural recovery, and their influence on printability. The effect of particle-size distribution on particle packing, densification, microstructure and mechanical performance is subsequently examined. Furthermore, vacuum-assisted colloidal silica infiltration is employed as a post-processing technique to reduce accessible porosity and enhance mechanical properties. The results demonstrate that particle characteristics significantly influence ink behaviour and final ceramic properties. Silica infiltration further improves the mechanical performance, with the maximum flexural strength reaching 241 MPa, representing an increase of approximately 236% compared with the corresponding uninfiltrated sample. The findings provide insights into the processing–structure–property relationships governing DIW-fabricated alumina ceramics and establish the potential of particle engineering and infiltration for improving their performance.
keywords: 3D printing; rheology; vacuum infiltration; alumina; flexural strength

name: Himani Mattoo
thesis_title: ROBUST DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM STATE ESTIMATION AND TOPOLOGY DETECTION CONSIDERING ASYNCHRONOUS HETEROGENEOUS MEASUREMENTS
abstract:
Modern distribution systems face increasing challenges in reliable monitoring and state estimation due to high distributed energy resource penetration, heterogeneous asynchronous measurements, non-Gaussian noise, missing data, cyberattacks, and frequent network reconfiguration.
The work develops robust, scalable, and data-driven frameworks for state estimation, anomaly detection, and topology identification in active distribution networks. First, a modular forecasting-aided state estimation framework is proposed to fuse asynchronous, multi-rate measurements from µPMUs, RTUs, and smart meters. Its two-level architecture separates local asynchrony handling from global data fusion, eliminating the need for global time synchronization.
Second, a data-driven gradient optimization-based DSSE method is developed using gradient-boosting regression trees and residual-based learning to address non-Gaussian noise, missing measurements, outliers, and abrupt load variations. A closed-form Cramér–Rao lower bound under Laplacian noise is derived to establish theoretical performance limits.
Third, a weighted Mahalanobis distance-based gradient-boosting framework is introduced to detect and mitigate GPS-spoofing attacks in PMU measurements.
Finally, an attention-enhanced physics-informed spatio-temporal graph neural network is developed for topology detection and state estimation under switching events, PMU failures, bad data, and photovoltaic variability.
All frameworks are validated on standard IEEE distribution test systems, demonstrating improved accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency for resilient monitoring of future smart distribution networks.
keywords: Distribution System State Estimation; Forecasting-Aided State Estimation ; Asynchronous Heterogeneous Measurements; Non-Gaussian Noise; Cybersecurity; Physics-Informed Graph Neural Networks; Active Distribution Networks; Machine Learning

name: Himanshu Gupta
thesis_title: Chemical Characterization, Source Apportionment, and Risk Assessment of Ambient Particulate Matter and Road Dust in Urban and Rural Assam
abstract: My doctoral research investigates the chemical composition, emission sources, atmospheric transport, spatial distribution, and health implications of particulate matter in urban Guwahati and rural Nalbari, Assam. Ambient PM2.5 and PM10, together with road dust, were systematically sampled and analysed for trace elements, water-soluble ions, and carbonaceous fractions using ICP-MS, ion chromatography, and total organic carbon analysis. Positive Matrix Factorization was applied to identify and quantify major sources, while Conditional Bivariate Probability Function analysis examined their directional influence. HYSPLIT backward trajectories assessed regional air-mass transport, and GIS-based inverse distance weighting evaluated spatial variations and pollution hotspots. The study identified road dust and construction as the dominant source, accompanied by vehicular emissions, industrial activities, biomass burning, and secondary aerosol formation. Health-risk assessment evaluated inhalation, ingestion, and dermal exposure to toxic elements among children and adults, with children generally showing greater vulnerability. The integrated findings distinguish urban and rural pollution characteristics and link measured chemical constituents with their probable sources, transport pathways, spatial patterns, and health relevance. The research provides a scientific basis for prioritising emission sources, protecting vulnerable populations, and supporting locally appropriate, evidence-based air-quality management and mitigation strategies for Assam and other rapidly developing regions within Northeast India's changing environmental context.
keywords: Air Pollution; Particulate Matter; Chemical Characterization; Trace Elements; Source Apportionment; Positive Matrix Factorization; Atmospheric Transport; Spatial Analysis; Health Risk Assessment; Air Quality Management

name: HIMANSHU SHARMA
thesis_title: Sensing Sleep Apnea from Sound, Speech and Physiology signals: A Study on Public and Indian Clinical Data
abstract: My Ph.D. research at IIT Guwahati develops deep learning methods for speech, audio and physiological signal analysis, applied to non-invasive screening of sleep-disordered breathing such as obstructive sleep apnea. I design end-to-end pipelines that learn from nocturnal respiratory acoustics, including tracheal audio and snoring, together with airflow, oximetry and cardiovascular signals from polysomnography. My work combines spectral feature learning (MFCC, log-Mel) with CNN, ResNet and MobileNet architectures, and fine-tuning of self-supervised speech foundation models such as Wav2Vec 2.0, WavLM, HuBERT and Whisper. Key contributions include CAAM-Net, a lightweight attention-based model for snore-based apnea screening; SnoreFlowNet, which fuses snore-intensity and airflow dynamics with cardiovascular signals; TrachEventNet, for full-night apnea–hypopnea event localization and event-burden estimation; and a multi-encoder framework for cross-device respiratory audio. I also study how clinically relevant information emerges across the layers of pretrained audio encoders, and I am collecting in collaboration with Medical Clinic a multilingual (English, Hindi, Telugu) wake-speech dataset to investigate speech biomarkers of sleep apnea. Collaborative work extends these methods to stuttering detection. Along with prior industry experience of 1.5 years in data analytics, I seek industry and research roles in speech and audio AI, healthcare AI and applied machine learning.

name: HIRAK JYOTI BAISHYA
thesis_title: In Silico Drug Discovery Against Two Major Infectious Diseases: COVID-19 and Malaria
abstract: My research focuses on computational drug discovery and molecular modelling, particularly the identification and evaluation of potential therapeutic candidates against infectious diseases. My doctoral research, titled “In Silico Drug Discovery Against Two Major Infectious Diseases: COVID-19 and Malaria,” involves structure-based drug design, molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, binding free-energy calculations (MM/GBSA), and density functional theory (DFT) studies. I have investigated potential inhibitors targeting SARS-CoV-2 proteins, including the spike protein receptor-binding domain (RBD) using ?-lactam compounds and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) using synthetic and designer unnatural nucleoside analogues. My research also explores unnatural nucleosides as potential inhibitors of Plasmodium falciparum purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PfPNP), incorporating DFT-based reaction-mechanism and activation-barrier studies. My broader research interests include computational chemistry, protein-ligand interactions, molecular recognition, protein dynamics, and the application of computational approaches to rational drug design and discovery.

name: Imran Hussain
thesis_title: Development of BTCA-Doped Polyaniline Hybrid Nanocomposites with 2D Nanomaterials and Carbon Fillers for Advanced Energy Storage and printable ink for EMI Shielding Applications
abstract:
Conventional conducting polymer electrodes suffer from rapid capacity fading, volumetric swelling, and poor multi-functional integration, while sustainable approaches for simultaneously optimizing high-performance energy storage and electromagnetic attenuation remain underexplored.
This research focuses on the design, synthesis and optimization of advanced functional nanocomposites tailored for high-performance energy storage and electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding applications. A primary methodology involves the in-situ oxidative polymerization of benzene-1, 2, 4, 5-tetracarboxylic acid (BTCA)-functionalized polyaniline (PANI) hybridized with diverse 2D nanofillers, including graphene derivatives, molybdenum disulfide MoS2 (bulk and exfoliated) and delaminated Ti3C2Tx MXene. Multifunctional organic dopant and structure-directing agent, BTCA promotes robust ?-? interchain stacking, extended conjugation length, and superior thermal resilience. Solution-processable composite inks exhibit exceptional specific capacitances, robust energy densities, and outstanding cyclic stability over thousands of cycles-while simultaneously delivering absorption-dominated EMI shielding effectiveness across the X and Ku frequency bands. The experimental characterization was supported by morphological and structural analysis using FESEM, FETEM, HRTEM, Raman, FTIR, XRD, and SAED, elemental mapping via EDX and STEM, electrochemical evaluations using Gamry 600 and Admiral Squidstat workstations, and EMI shielding testing via VNA. These robust, dual-functional nanocomposites pave the way for next-generation flexible electronics, self-powered energy storage systems, and advanced EMI shielding materials.
keywords: Conducting Polymers; 2D materials; In-situ oxidative polymerization; EDLC; Supercapacitors; Electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding; X-band and Ku-band attenuation; Dielectric loss; X-band and Ku-band attenuation

name: Janga Venkatesh
thesis_title: Design, modelling, simulation, and experimental validation of an integrated process for microplastic-free sea salt production
abstract:
Microplastic contamination in salt production is an emerging concern because conventional seawater treatment and crystallization may not prevent microplastics from entering the final product. This thesis investigates microplastic behaviour, removal, and entrapment during sodium chloride production and develops an integrated framework for producing microplastic-free salt.
A ceramic ultrafiltration (UF) membrane with a nominal pore size of 20 nm reduced microplastic concentration from 6,760 ± 311 to 188 ± 25 particles L?¹, corresponding to 97.22% rejection. The effects of feed volume, mother-liquor concentration, and cooling conditions on microplastic incorporation during evaporation-crystallization were investigated. Higher mother-liquor concentration and slower cooling promoted microplastic entrapment in the crystallized salt. Sequential evaporation-crystallization was then assessed using two pretreatment routes: UF and sedimentation.
A dynamic mechanistic Modelica model was developed to describe evaporation, supersaturation, nucleation, crystal growth, and microplastic entrapment, and was validated against experimental observations. The study also employs automated image analysis for particle quantification. Aspen Plus simulation evaluated industrial-scale performance at a feed capacity of 1,000 L h?¹, followed by techno-economic assessment. The UF-integrated process recovered 66.14% of the salt as microplastic-free product. Overall, this work provides experimental, modelling, and process-design insights for improving salt quality and advancing sustainable microplastic-control strategies in salt production.
keywords: Microplastics; Sodium chloride production; Ceramic ultrafiltration; Sedimentation; Sequential evaporation-crystallization; Microplastic entrapment; Dynamic modelling; Modelica; Dymola; Aspen Plus; Python; MATLAB; Techno-economic analysis

name: Jay Deep Kalita
thesis_title: Bridging As-Planned and As-Built: BIM-Based Augmented Reality and Computer Vision for Automated Construction Monitoring
abstract: Automation in Construction remains limited for reinforced-concrete works, where progress and quality are still verified manually against 2D drawings. This research develops a BIM Digital Twin framework that integrates Augmented Reality in Construction, Computer Vision in Monitoring and Automatic Schedule Generation. First, a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) algorithm extracts geometric adjacency and precedence constraints among BIM elements, including embedded rebar, enabling Automatic Schedule Generation; for a G+2 structure, it produced a validated 3,275-task schedule with a 130-fold computational speed-up over pairwise O(n²) comparison. Second, the 4D BIM model is segmented into date-specific glTF models and rendered through a WebXR hit-test-based AR application, with on-site progress synchronised to MS Project via a Python server and VBA. Third, Rebar Progress Monitoring is achieved through a BIM-AR-CV pipeline that compares camera frames pixel by pixel with AR mask images using Canny edge detection, HSV segmentation and K-means clustering. Occlusion is addressed by multi-view evidence accumulation, increasing verified elements from 10/17 to 23/30. To extend this pipeline, Model Training of a YOLO11 CNN-based instance-segmentation network was carried out, with the model tested and validated on annotated image data. The framework enables low-cost, real-time construction monitoring on handheld devices.
keywords: Augmented Reality in Construction; Automation in Construction; Computer vision in Monitoring; Rebar progress monitoring, CNN; Model training; Automatic schedule generation; BIM digital twin

name: Jenny Laura R V S
thesis_title: Parametric Evaluation of Local Site Effects in Northern Bihar via Ground Response Analysis and Genetic Programming Based Extrapolation of Dynamic Soil Properties
abstract: The proximity of northern Bihar to the great Himalayan collision arc exposes the region to hundreds of moderate to great earthquakes (EQs). Owing to the prospect of future major EQs in the central seismic gap, the insights on local site effect (LSE) of northern Bihar is the need of the hour to improve hazard management. Seventy locations in Madhubani, Darbhanga and Sitamarhi—the locations exposed to liquefaction due to 1934 and 2015 EQs, are investigated using SPT (20 locations) and MASW (50 locations) testing. The shear wave velocity (Vs) profiles and SPT-N obtained are utilized to perform site characterization. The 70 Vs and SPT-N profiles are extrapolated till 100 m using empirical extrapolation methods to establish uniform extrapolated soil profiles (ESP). The ESPs are utilized to perform equivalent linear ground response analysis (ELGRA) using DSPCs and 62 scenario-based synthetic ground motions (GMs). The influence of the soil and GM parameters on LSE is studied, and decision boundaries are stipulated. Correlations for shear strain as a function of the influencing parameters are proposed for the ease of future utility. Further, limitations in adapting empirical extrapolation methods are rectified using genetic programming to arrive at a better refined ESP.
keywords: Geotechnical Earthquake Engineering; Subsurface Investigation; Multichannel Analysis of Surface Wave (MASW); Standard Penetration Test (SPT); Genetic Programming; Seismic Hazard; Site Classification; DEEPSOIL

name: Joyshree Chakraborty
discipline: Centre for Linguistic Science and Technology
thesis_title: Detecting L2 Hindi: The Case of Assamese Speakers Speaking Hindi
abstract:
This research focuses on developing robust and inclusive speech technologies through Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Natural Language Processing (NLP), with particular emphasis on accented speech recognition and computational speech analysis. The study investigates the influence of Assamese (L1) on Hindi (L2) and its implications for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems.
Key contributions include developing speech datasets, including a spontaneous Assamese-accented Hindi corpus comprising 103 speakers, and designing computational frameworks for accent identification and speech analysis. By fine-tuning a pretrained Wav2Vec2 model, the research reduced Word Error Rate (WER) from 30.15% to 6.88%, demonstrating effective adaptation of deep learning models to accented speech.
The work further explores acoustic feature extraction, prosodic modeling, Rhythm Formant Analysis (RFA), and machine learning classifiers. Combining MFCC and RFA features with Support Vector Machines achieved 76% accuracy in three-class accent classification. Additionally, latent speech embeddings were investigated to identify language-specific prosodic characteristics, alongside the deployment of a web-based accent identification system. Overall, this research demonstrates practical expertise in speech AI, data-driven modeling, transfer learning, feature engineering, model evaluation, and deployment, contributing to multilingual speech technologies and real-world AI applications.

name: JYOTI PRAKASH RAY
thesis_title: Polymer-Nanocomposites Catalysed Photocatalytic Process for Degradation and Mineralisation of Recalcitrant Pollutants: Synthesis, Characterisation and Toxicological Assessment
abstract: The increasing presence of persistent organic pollutants in aquatic environments has emerged as a major environmental concern, necessitating the development of efficient and sustainable wastewater treatment technologies. This doctoral research focuses on the development of semiconductor-based nanocomposite photocatalysts for the degradation of major classes of contaminants under light irradiation. The study involves the synthesis and physicochemical characterisation of advanced photocatalytic materials, followed by systematic evaluation of their photocatalytic performance, degradation kinetics, and underlying reaction mechanisms both in simulated water and in a real-time river water matrix. Particular emphasis is placed on improving visible-light utilisation, charge-carrier separation, reactive oxygen species generation, and catalyst stability for enhanced pollutant removal. Furthermore, the degradation pathways and formation of intermediate products are investigated to understand the transformation of target pollutants during treatment. Beyond assessing degradation efficiency, the research incorporates ecotoxicological evaluation to investigate the potential environmental impacts of treated water and degradation intermediates using biological models. The overall study aims to integrate nanotechnology, environmental biotechnology, and photocatalytic engineering to develop efficient, reusable, and environmentally sustainable approaches for wastewater remediation and aquatic ecosystem protection.
keywords: Environmental Biotechnology; Advanced Oxidation Processes (AOPs); Photocatalysis; Nanotechnology & Nanomaterials; Sustainable Wastewater Treatment; Environmental Remediation; Water Quality Assessment; Materials Characterization; Environmental Sustainability; Process Optimization

name: Kanak Jindal
thesis_title: Development of Continuous Toolpaths for Additive Manufacturing
abstract: This thesis addresses two aspects of additive manufacturing: the planning of the deposition process and the machine that carries it out. Conventional slicing software generates toolpaths that repeatedly interrupt material flow, introducing defects and increasing build time. A toolpath generation method based on the Travelling Salesman Problem was developed to produce a single, continuous path for each layer, eliminating retractions and allowing the direction of material deposition to be controlled. Custom G-code was developed to print parts with this method on a commercial fused filament fabrication (FFF) printer, and the printed components were evaluated through tensile, compression, flexural and torsion testing. The results demonstrate that the strength and stiffness of a part can be tailored to its service loading through the toolpath alone, without any change in material or equipment. In torsion, the stiffness of printed shafts more than doubled across the toolpath strategies examined. In parallel, a novel 5-axis hybrid scissor-based machine tool for additive manufacturing was designed and developed, encompassing concept design, kinematic modelling, fabrication, assembly and commissioning. The work integrates algorithm development, mechanical design, prototype development and experimental validation.
keywords: Toolpath Planning; Custom G-code Generation; Mechanism Design; Mechanical System Design

name: Kapil Kumar Sahu
thesis_title: Design and Analysis of Fractional Order Internal Model Control (IMC) Strategy for Higher-Order Processes with/without Non-Minimum Phase (NMP).
abstract: This research focuses on developing optimization-based Fractional-Order Internal Model Control (FO-IMC) strategies for challenging chemical processes. A three-parameter fractional-order filter, characterized by \(\lambda\), \(\beta\), and \(\alpha\), is simultaneously tuned using Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Penalty-based objective functions are formulated to balance tracking performance, overshoot, rise time, and settling time. The proposed framework is evaluated for higher-order, time-delay, non-minimum-phase, and unstable processes. Servo tracking, disturbance rejection, stability, and robustness under process parameter variations are investigated to establish a systematic approach for improved chemical process control.
keywords: Fractional-Order IMC; Particle Swarm Optimization; Controller Optimization; Chemical Process Control; Time-Delay Systems; Non-Minimum-Phase Processes; Unstable Processes; Robustness

name: Kavyashree Venkatesh
thesis_title: Supporting Co-design for Children with special needs: Designing smart assistive solutions for emerging economies
abstract: Designing smart and customisable assistive solutions (devices, technologies, and services) is a complex endeavour. It demands collaborative design approaches, multi-disciplinary expertise, and above all, empathising with users with special needs. This poses profound challenges for designers, innovators and entrepreneurs in various aspects of productisation (design, development, and deployment).  Co-design is considered the best-suited approach for designing such systems where user groups are little or not well understood. However, it is rarely adopted for designing customisable ADs, though several studies have employed co-design approaches for other product solutions in various capacities for special needs. This research investigates co-design as the vehicle to engage multiple stakeholders and users, with diverse needs, abilities, characteristics and expertise, and, further prescribes a process support, ‘mCoDe’, for designers to undertake ‘multi-user-centric co-design’ of assistive devices for special needs groups, like children who require a ‘voice’ on their behalf. The research addresses a critical challenge in socio-technical systems, enabling effective collaboration among diverse stakeholders to address complex societal issues such as healthcare accessibility, ageing populations, assistive technologies, and community well-being.
keywords: assistive technology; inclusive design; design research; biomedical; healthcare innovation; product design; product management; medical device; user research; sustainability; rehabilitation engineering;

name: Khalid Jamal Ansari
thesis_title: Investigation of electric field-induced lithography in a high dielectric environment and noisy field
abstract: The research focuses on electric field-induced patterning, commonly known as electrohydrodynamic (EHD) patterning, which offers a versatile approach to fabricating micro- and nanoscale surface patterns via electric-field-driven instabilities in polymer thin films. This study investigates the influence of high-dielectric environments (e.g., liquid crystals) and noisy electric fields (using white noise) on the EHD patterning behaviour of thin polymer films. A high-dielectric environment is explored as a means of modifying the electric field distribution and electrohydrodynamic interactions at the polymer interface, potentially providing additional control over pattern formation and characteristic length scales. Furthermore, the application of noisy electric fields introduces temporal fluctuations that may alter the growth dynamics, spatial organization, and uniformity of the resulting structures. The investigation provides insights into controlling surface instabilities beyond conventional uniform-field approaches and explores new possibilities for tuning pattern dimensions, structural organization, and defect formation. These findings may contribute to the development of versatile and adaptable lithographic strategies for advanced micro- and nanostructured surfaces. The resulting structures may have applications in areas such as biomimetics and photonics etc.
keywords: Electrohydrdynamic Patterning; Liquid Crystals; Noisy Field; Biomimetics; Photonics

name: Koushik Bhakta
thesis_title: Quantum state transfer in Grover walks on graphs
abstract: The thesis studies perfect state transfer in Grover walks on finite graphs, a discrete-time model of quantum evolution motivated by quantum communication. We investigate when a state associated with one vertex can be transferred exactly to a state associated with another vertex after some time. Our approach is based on algebraic graph theory. We study transfer between vertex states through the normalized adjacency matrix, its eigenvalues and spectral projections, and Chebyshev polynomials. These tools connect the dynamics of the walk with the structural and arithmetic properties of the underlying graph. We also examine the relationship between perfect state transfer and periodicity. The investigation covers Cayley graphs over finite abelian groups, Cayley graphs over dihedral groups, generalized Bethe trees, and graphs belonging to association schemes. Group characters and representations, the level structure of trees, and common eigenspace decompositions provide methods for studying transfer in these families. We focus on the conditions that permit transfer, the vertices involved, and the possible transfer times. By examining these different settings within a common spectral framework, this thesis explores how graph structure governs exact quantum state transfer and contributes to the mathematical understanding of information transport in discrete-time quantum walks.
keywords: Algebraic graph theory; Quantum computing; Cayley graph; Association scheme

name: KOUSHIK JENA
thesis_title: Techno-commercial assessment of microwave drying for the preparation of sprouted little millet (Panicum sumatrense) flour with better nutritional and functional properties".
abstract: Little millet (Panicum sumatrense) is one of the important minor millets, oval to elliptical in shape and grey to straw-white in color, and is rich in dietary fiber, protein, various phytochemicals, and minerals. But its consumption is limited by a lack of processing technologies to enhance its nutritional value. Sprouting is a potent traditional processing technique that enhances the nutritional composition by reducing antinutritional content. After sprouting, drying is essential to improve the storage stability of the flour. Controlled microwave drying is an efficient technology that not only greatly reduces drying time but also preserves nutritional quality.  In the present study, little millets were sprouted at 30 ? and 90% relative humidity for 72 h. Then, sprouted little millets were dried in a laboratory-scale controlled microwave at three power levels of 450 (MW-450), 750 (MW-750), and 1050 Watt (MW-1050), with the upper temperature set at 50 ? to avoid overheating of the product. The physicochemical properties, along with storage stability studies, of the microwave-dried flour were compared with those of the hot-air oven-dried sprouted little millet flour at 50 ? (HA-50) and of native, unprocessed little millet flour (NA). The techno-economic study was used to evaluate the process's feasibility.
keywords: Microwave processing; Little millet; Sprouting; Antinutrients; Rheological studies

name: Koyel Mukherjee
discipline: Centre for Linguistic Science and Technology
thesis_title: Constructing Visual Meaning: Metaphor, Convention, and Continuity Across Visual Forms
abstract: While visual meaning can seem immediate or perceptual, this thesis argues that it is actively constructed through structural organization, figurative extension, attentional focus, conventions, and contextual grounding. By examining 2D visual forms such as schematic faces, comic-strip narratives, and emojis, it analyzes how viewers interpret visual meaning, including the combination of graphical components, visual navigation, and the interplay between visual signs and language. Five experiments using behavioral responses, eye-tracking, pupillometry, semantic-fit judgments, and subjective ratings produced convergent findings: incongruent schematic faces increase processing demands, comic layouts direct attention and continuity, and emojis display graded integration across literal, figurative, and contextual meanings. Processing difficulty reflects the mental effort to resolve mismatches, repair disruptions, and select contextually appropriate meanings. Integrating theoretical and experimental approaches from visual morphology, metaphor, event comprehension, multimodal analysis, and emoji studies, the thesis offers a cognitive-semiotic account of visual meaning. It shows that visual forms are understood as structured, meaning-bearing elements, and that contemporary visual communication emerges through the coordination of visual structure, attention, and conceptual interpretation.
keywords: Visual attention; Attentional allocation; Visual meaning construction; Multimodal integration; Eye-Tracking

name: Kumar Shanu
thesis_title: Studies on Poly (lactic acid)-based Blends,  Nanocomposites and Functional Polymeric  Materials
abstract: The development of sustainable, high-performance biodegradable polymers is important for reducing the environmental impact of plastic packaging. My research investigates polylactic acid (PLA)-based materials for food-packaging applications through molecular dynamics simulations and experimental studies. The computational work examines graphene oxide (GO)- and cellulose nanocrystal (CNC)-reinforced PLA nanocomposites, focusing on how filler loading, dimensions and structure influence material properties, free volume and the transport of oxygen, water and carbon dioxide. PLA–polybutylene adipate-co-terephthalate (PBAT) blends are investigated to understand their structural characteristics, miscibility and gas-transport behaviour. In addition, PLA–PBAT and PLA–polycaprolactone (PCL) systems are compared using experimental and computational approaches to relate molecular interactions and blend structure to material performance. A further part of the research explores umbelliferone-modified PLA, with an emphasis on photo-switchable crosslinking and decrosslinking. Molecular models and simulations are developed using LAMMPS and Materials Studio, supported by tools such as VMD and PACKMOL, while experimental investigations employ polymer processing and materials-characterization techniques. By combining atomistic modelling with experimental analysis, this work seeks to establish structure–property relationships and provide insights for designing improved biodegradable polymer blends and nanocomposites. The outcomes are relevant to sustainable polymer development, particularly the design of materials with controlled gas-transport and performance characteristics for packaging applications.
keywords: (Polylactic Acid; Molecular Dynamics Simulation; Polymer Nanocomposites; Graphene Oxide; Cellulose Nanocrystals; PLA–PBAT Blends; PLA–PCL Blends; Gas Diffusion; Biodegradable Polymers; Photo-Responsive Polymers)

name: Lakhi Narayan Bharadwaj
discipline: Department of Humanities and Social Sciences
thesis_title: Technological Change, Subcontracting Intensity and Labor Market Outcomes: Evidence from Indian Manufacturing Sector
abstract: Empirical evidence on technological change and labor market outcomes comes largely from developed countries, where studies typically examine the relationship between technology and employment and between technology and subcontracting separately. This study brings the two together for the Indian manufacturing sector over the period 2000-2023, examining whether technological change affects employment both directly and indirectly through subcontracting arrangements, and extends the analysis to the unorganized sector. Using ASI and NSSO data and the two-step system GMM estimator, it employs two measures of technological change: Hicks-neutral technological change, capturing overall technological progress, and the share of IT capital, capturing digital technology. The results show that Hicks-neutral technological change reduces employment in the contemporaneous period, whereas digital technology has no significant effect on employment. However, this negative effect is partly offset in the same period by an indirect positive effect operating through subcontracting intensity. Results for unorganized manufacturing are broadly similar, except that digital technology generates an indirect wage premium in that sector. These findings suggest that fears of job losses from digital technology may be overstated for Indian manufacturing, while subcontracting partly cushions the labor displacement caused by Hicks-neutral technological change.
keywords: Development Economics; Labor Economics; Industrial Economics; Applied Econometrics

name: Limashree Sahoo
thesis_title: Tuning Oxidative Reactivity Through Equatorial Ligand Modulation in Nonheme Metal-Oxygen Intermediates
abstract:
My doctoral research focuses on tuning the oxidative reactivity of non-heme transition-metal–oxygen intermediates through systematic modulation of primary and secondary coordination spheres. I investigate how equatorial ligand donor atoms influence the electronic structure, spin state, redox properties, stability, and reactivity of molecular iron and copper complexes relevant to dioxygen activation and biological oxidation chemistry.
A major component involves synthesizing and investigating N5-, N4S-, and N4O-supported iron complexes, particularly iron(IV)–oxo and iron(III)–alkylperoxo intermediates. Using UV–visible, resonance Raman, EPR, mass spectrometry, electrochemistry, and kinetic studies, I examine ligand-dependent changes in metal–oxygen bonding, spin states, stability, and oxidative reactivity. My studies also explore C–H oxidation, oxygen-atom transfer, and competing O–O and C–O bond cleavage pathways, including the influence of hydrogen bonding and secondary coordination environments.
Additionally, I have investigated ligand-controlled reaction pathways in non-heme iron-mediated chlorite oxidation, demonstrating how coordination-sphere modifications can influence electron-transfer and oxygen-atom-transfer processes. I have further extended this research to N-, S-, and O-modulated copper(II)–alkylperoxo complexes, establishing correlations between ligand donor properties, electronic structure, stability, and reactivity through spectroscopic, electrochemical, kinetic, and Hammett analyses.
keywords: Coordination chemistry; Bio-inspired chemistry; Non-heme metal-oxygen intermediates; Synthesis & characterization; Catalysis; Reaction mechanism; Spectroscopic techniques; Kinetics; Data analysis

name: Lwithwsa Swargiary
thesis_title: Studies of Linear and Nonlinear optical properties of Lithium Niobate and Lithium Tantalate thin films fabricated via Pulsed laser deposition and its application in sensing based on surface plasmon resonance
abstract: Thin film technology has become an essential platform for modern electronic, optoelectronic, photonic and sensing devices. Compared with bulk materials, thin films offer reduced material consumption, compact device architectures, tunable physical properties, high surface to volume ratios and compatibility with integrated fabrication. Their properties can be tailored through composition, thickness, deposition conditions and surface morphology. My research focuses on the fabrication, optimization and optical investigation of lithium tantalate (LT) and lithium niobate (LN) thin films using pulsed laser deposition. These materials exhibit a combination of nonlinear optical, electro-optic, piezoelectric, ferroelectric, pyroelectric and acousto-optic properties, making them promising candidates for integrated photonics and optoelectronic technologies. A major part of my work examines how deposition parameters influence the structural, morphological and optical properties of LT and LN thin films, with particular emphasis on their nonlinear optical response and photonic applications. My research also explores metallic nanostructure as platforms for controlling light–matter interactions. In particular, I investigate nanostructured silver thin films for plasmonic and lossy mode resonance studies and evaluate their potential for refractive-index sensing applications. These studies link processing, structure and optical response to future integrated photonic device applications.
keywords: Thin film characterisation; numerical modelling; optoelectronics; optical characterisation; material science; nanomaterials; nonlinear optics; plasmonics; laser; optical sensing

name: Mahendra Patel
thesis_title: A study on diaphragm wall support systems for deep excavation
abstract: The research investigates the performance, optimization, and long-term behavior of anchored diaphragm wall support systems for deep excavations in clayey and sandy soils. A systematic design-oriented numerical framework is developed that iteratively optimizes support system characteristics until the optimal configurations comply with serviceability and anchor safety limits. For both soil types, two representative excavation cases are examined through extensive parametric analyses using PLAXIS 2D and 3D. The 2D analyses examine the influence of different one-, two-, three-, and four-anchor layouts, anchor positions and vertical spacing, wall thickness, anchor prestress load, and longitudinal spacing, considering their individual and combined contributions to system performance. The performance difference between anchored and unanchored walls is also assessed. For clayey soils, consolidation analyses are conducted over excavation and post-excavation periods to investigate long-term behavior. 3D analyses further examine excavation length and corner effects, while the influence of excavation rates is evaluated across a wide range of soil permeability. The optimization framework is subsequently applied to sandy soils, and the optimized configurations are extended to 3D analyses. A comparative assessment of clayey and sandy soils elucidates differences in drainage characteristics, pore-pressure response, underlying mechanisms and optimal support configurations.
keywords: Deep Excavation; Retaining Structures; 2D & 3D Finite Element Analysis; Diaphragm Walls; Ground Anchors; Soil-Structure Interaction; Underground Infrastructure; Stiff clay; Consolidation; Sandy soil.

name: MALAY KUMAR BAROI
thesis_title: Supramolecular Chemical Ligation (SCL) : A proof of concept and its Application

name: Mane Pooja
thesis_title: Deep Learning for Retinal Analysis from Optical Coherence Tomography Images and Volumes
abstract: My Ph.D. research focuses on developing deep?learning techniques for automated and quantitative analysis of retinal structure and vasculature using optical coherence tomography (OCT) and optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA). The core novelty lies in designing efficient and robust architectures capable of processing both 2D and 3D OCT/OCTA data for retinal and vascular segmentation, quantitative biomarker extraction, disease classification, and multimodal multitask learning. By emphasizing computational efficiency, these models enable accurate and reliable analysis of complex retinal imaging data while reducing inference time and resource demands, supporting their deployment in clinical and resource?constrained healthcare environments.
keywords: AI for Biomedical Imaging, Retinal OCT/OCTA Analysis, Image Segmentation and Reconstruction, Multimodal Deep Learning, 3D Image Analysis,  Signal Processing.

name: MANGAL
thesis_title: Bio-Based Polyurethane Composites from Renewable Vegetable Oils: Synthesis, Reinforcement, Characterization, and Molecular-Level Insights
abstract: This thesis focuses on the development of sustainable, high-performance bio-based polyurethane (PU) materials using renewable castor oil and hydroxylated linseed oil, with hexamethylene diisocyanate (HDI) as the crosslinking agent. A catalyst-free, one-pot synthesis approach was employed to fabricate polyurethane sheets and nanocomposite films reinforced with cellulose nanofibers (CNF), Bhimal-fiber-derived activated carbon (BFAC), and carboxyl-functionalized multi-walled carbon nanotubes (COOH-MWCNTs). Comprehensive experimental characterization and density functional theory (DFT) calculations were integrated to establish structure–property relationships and elucidate molecular interactions and reaction mechanisms. The optimized castor-oil PU/CNF composite achieved a tensile strength of 22.55 MPa and 55.9% elongation, while COOH-MWCNT reinforcement increased tensile strength from 12.08 to 25.26 MPa and fracture strain from 22.65% to 60.92%. BFAC-reinforced PU coatings demonstrated enhanced corrosion protection, achieving impedance-based inhibition efficiency exceeding 96% at 5 wt% BFAC loading. Advanced thermal, mechanical, morphological, spectroscopic and electrochemical analyses, supported by DFT, PES and IRC calculations, provided insights into material performance and molecular-level interactions. This research establishes a versatile renewable polyurethane platform with significant potential for sustainable polymer composites, high-performance coating technologies, flexible materials and industrial anticorrosion applications.
keywords: Bio-Based Polyurethane; Renewable Vegetable Oils; Nanocomposites; Cellulose Nanofibers; Activated Carbon; Multi-Walled Carbon Nanotubes; Density Functional Theory

name: MD BADIRUJJAMAN
thesis_title: Development of stimuli-responsive prodrugs for the sustained delivery of chemotherapeutic drug.
abstract: I am currently working on the development of stimuli-responsive prodrugs of chemotherapeutic drug for the better treatment of cancer. Prodrugs are synthesized using multi-step organic synthesis. After synthesis, activation of prodrugs in the presence of respective stimuli are investigated using UV-vis and fluorescence spectroscopy. Release of chemotherapeutic drug from the prodrugs are monitored using standard HPLC method. In addition, details mechanistic anticancer activity of prodrugs are evaluated to understand the efficacy of prodrug to treatment of cancer using human cancer model.
keywords: Organic chemistry, Multi-step organic synthesis, prodrug chemistry, biochemical, Cell culture, Handling of cancer cells

name: MEERA G NAIR
thesis_title: Coupled Peridynamics and Damage Mechanics Framework for Failure Analysis of Metallic and Composite Structures
abstract: Accurate prediction of failure in metals and composites is essential for the safe and efficient design of engineering structures across industries. My doctoral research at IIT Guwahati addresses this using peridynamics (PD), a nonlocal theory that naturally captures discontinuities and damage, though at a higher computational cost. In-house PD and finite element solvers were developed in MATLAB, along with elastic and elastoplastic PD models incorporating isotropic, kinematic and mixed hardening, including a new elastoplastic PD model for composites. To improve efficiency, PD was coupled with the finite element method (FEM), restricting PD to critical regions, and with continuum damage mechanics (CDM) for damage analysis. These frameworks were applied to bimaterial plates, GLARE fibre metal laminates and free edge delamination in composite laminates, and validated against analytical, experimental and Abaqus results. Beyond my doctoral work, I carried out structural design, optimization and analysis of launch vehicle isogrid interstage structures at VSSC (ISRO). As Mechanical Team Lead for the COSPAR-1 3U CubeSat at HEX20, I directed the mechanical design, fabrication and AIVT of flight hardware. This blend of advanced numerical modelling and hands-on hardware development equips me to address real-world structural engineering challenges.

name: Mekala Anil Kumar
thesis_title: Advanced Viscoelastic Composites for Structural Applications: Material Characterisation, Dynamic Modelling, and Performance Evaluation
abstract: The present research focuses on the development, modelling, and dynamic investigation of advanced viscoelastic composite materials and structures for improved vibration attenuation and structural performance. The study explores the influence of material reinforcement, structural configuration, and viscoelastic properties on the dynamic response of composite systems. Initially, nanofiller-reinforced viscoelastic nanocomposites incorporating carbon black and graphene nanoplatelets are investigated to understand their constitutive behaviour and vibration damping capabilities. Their applications are further examined in sandwich beams and plates, including active constrained layer damping configurations and axially graded viscoelastic cores. The research is also extended to corrugated composite structures incorporating viscoelastic patches and hybrid composite-core configurations to investigate their structural and dynamic characteristics. Furthermore, fibre-reinforced viscoelastic composites are considered through constitutive modelling and homogenisation approaches to represent their effective material behaviour. Finite element formulations and computational techniques are employed to investigate the static and dynamic responses, vibration characteristics, and nonlinear behaviour of these structures, including parametric instability. Experimental characterisation and numerical investigations are used to evaluate the influence of material composition and structural parameters on the overall performance. The outcomes of this research are expected to contribute to the development of advanced viscoelastic composite systems with improved vibration attenuation capabilities and enhanced structural dynamic performance.
keywords: Viscoelastic composites; Viscoelastic nanocomposites; Carbon black; Graphene nanoplatelets; Fibre-reinforced composites; Homogenisation; Sandwich structures; Corrugated structures; Vibration damping; Active constrained layer damping; Finite element analysis; Nonlinear dynamics; Parametric instability

name: Mohit Kumar
discipline: School of Energy Science and Engineering
thesis_title: Hydrogen generation through an integrated photovoltaic cum electrolysis cell to generate power through a fuel cell device
abstract: The transition toward clean and sustainable energy systems is imperative to ensure long-term environmental, economic, and societal resilience. However, most currently utilized energy sources are associated with significant carbon dioxide emissions and limited sustainability, highlighting the urgent need for renewable, scalable, and low-carbon alternatives. In this context, hydrogen has emerged as a promising energy carrier, particularly when produced through water electrolysis powered by renewable electricity. Efficient water electrolysis depends critically on the development of highly active and durable electrocatalysts, suitable electrolytes, and optimized operating conditions to achieve high hydrogen production efficiency. This work is about setting up a solar cell setup with a rechargeable battery and designing an electrolysis cell. Further, an electrocatalyst was designed, which was integrated in the electrolysis cell to produce green hydrogen. The produced green hydrogen was supplied to a hydrogen fuel cell to generate power. This is how the photovoltaic system was integrated with a designed electrolysis cell and hydrogen fuel cell to generate power.
keywords: Electrolysis; water splitting; green Hydrogen; hydrogen fuel cell; Electrocatalyst. Solar driven water splitting.

name: Monish Goswami
thesis_title: Integrated Aprroaches for Sustainable Treatment and Resource Recovery from High-Concentration Swine Wastewater under Tropical Conditions
abstract: High-strength swine wastewater presents significant challenges for decentralised treatment owing to elevated organic matter, suspended solids, nutrients, pathogens, and veterinary antibiotics. This thesis investigates sustainable physicochemical and biological treatment approaches under tropical conditions, emphasising process optimisation, pollutant transformation, and resource recovery. Two independent physicochemical pathways were investigated: electrocoagulation followed by activated-carbon adsorption, and alum-based coagulation–flocculation with sludge valorisation through brick manufacturing. The principal biological treatment pathway comprised primary settling tank (PST) ? fixed-film upflow anaerobic reactor (FFUAR) ? alternative nature-based post-treatment systems. Initially, FFUAR performance was investigated under varying organic loading rates. Subsequent operational challenges motivated the development of a baffled PST for enhanced solids separation, with recovered sludge utilised for anaerobic methane production. The FFUAR was further evaluated through hydraulic retention time optimisation, kinetic modelling, and height-resolved investigations of biofilm characteristics, microbial succession, and antibiotic attenuation. Anaerobically treated effluent underwent separate polishing investigations using macrophyte-assisted vermifiltration, compared against conventional vermifiltration, and a baffled subsurface-flow constructed wetland. The central novelty lies in integrating operational improvements with mechanistic understanding, sludge-to-energy recovery, and alternative nature-based polishing pathways. Finally, treatment configurations were compared based on performance, estimated costs, land requirements, and electricity consumption to assess decentralised applicability.
keywords: wastewater treatment; anaerobic bioreactors; constructed wetlands; vermifiltration; sludge management; anaerobic digestion

name: Mouli Sarkar
thesis_title: Systems Pharmacology Framework for Identifying Disease-Modifying Interventions in Parkinson's Disease
abstract: Long-term Levodopa (L-DOPA) therapy for Parkinson’s disease (PD) is limited by rapid systemic metabolism, auto-oxidation and pulsatile dopaminergic stimulation, causing neurotoxicity without arresting neurodegeneration. We present a systems pharmacology framework for low-toxicity, multi-target, disease-modifying interventions. Network analysis identified bioactive phytocompounds whose in vitro validation in neuronal cells showed rescued mitochondrial bioenergetics, modulated stress-associated transcriptomic signatures and neuroprotection via N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor-associated pathways. Extending this pipeline, rationally designed dipeptides and pseudopeptides mitigated neurotoxicity by targeting lipid biosynthesis networks and Nuclear Factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B-cells (NF-?B) signalling. A network medicine analysis of L-DOPA-rich botanicals, integrating tissue-specific cis-eQTL single-nucleotide polymorphism data with metabolite-targeted hub nodes, revealed synergistic mechanisms regulating glutamate clearance, synaptic transmission and mitochondrial bioenergetics, supporting rational metabolic partners for L-DOPA against motor and non-motor symptoms. Finally, de novo peptide-L-DOPA conjugates were serum-stable, enzymatically resistant and selectively engaged blood-brain barrier transport proteins, enabling efficient central nervous system delivery without compromising potency. Together, these findings integrate network biology, multi-omics and experimental validation, offering a versatile route to lead optimisation and disease-modifying therapeutics.
keywords: Computational Drug Discovery; Network Pharmacology; Systems Biology; Bioinformatics; Multi-omics Data Analysis; RNA-seq Analysis; Molecular Docking; Molecular Dynamics Simulation; De Novo Peptide Design; Peptide Synthesis; Cheminformatics; Drug Repositioning; Neurodegenerative Diseases; Parkinson’s Disease

name: MUKESH BHARTI
thesis_title: Development and Performance Evaluation of a Rotating-Anode Electrocoagulation System with Hybrid Electrodes for the Treatment of Arsenic- and Fluoride-Contaminated Groundwater and Ni–Co–Mn-Bearing Wastewater
abstract: Arsenic and fluoride contamination of groundwater is a serious public health concern, particularly in rural India, while industrial effluents containing nickel, cobalt, and manganese pose additional environmental risks. Conventional treatment methods often require high chemical consumption, produce large sludge volumes, and are poorly suited for decentralized use. This research presents the design, development, and performance evaluation of a rotating-anode electrocoagulation system with hybrid electrodes for treating arsenic- and fluoride-contaminated groundwater and Ni–Co–Mn-bearing wastewater. In this system, coagulants are generated in situ by electrochemical dissolution of the anode, eliminating the need for external chemical dosing, while anode rotation is intended to improve mass transfer and contaminant removal. The effects of key operating parameters, including current density, inter-electrode distance, rotational speed, treatment time, pH, and electrode geometry, were systematically investigated to identify optimal conditions. Reaction kinetics, energy consumption, and techno-economic feasibility were evaluated for simultaneous arsenate and fluoride removal. Supporting analyses using ICP-MS, ion chromatography, FTIR, XRD, FESEM-EDX, and BET characterization were conducted to elucidate the removal mechanisms. The results establish rotating-anode electrocoagulation as a promising, low-cost technology for producing safe drinking water and treating heavy-metal-bearing industrial wastewater, with strong potential for community-scale implementation.
keywords: Electrocoagulation; Rotating Anode; Arsenic Removal; Fluoride Removal; Heavy Metal Wastewater Treatment; Techno-Economic Evaluation

name: Nabajyoti Nath
thesis_title: Performance Analysis of Underwater Wireless Communications using Acoustic and Optical Carriers
abstract: Underwater wireless communication is essential for ocean monitoring, surveillance and offshore exploration. Radio frequency waves suffer severe attenuation in seawater, so this thesis analyses underwater acoustic and optical communication systems. First, a comprehensive acoustic channel model is developed using BELLHOP with Argo sound speed profiles, surface altimetry and seabed bathymetry. Statistical analysis of wideband channel gains across 30 Indian Ocean coordinates shows the log-normal distribution gives the best fit, while Rayleigh fits poorly, and channel statistics vary with location. Intrapaths are added to dominant BELLHOP arrivals to capture small-scale scattering. Second, time reversal communication is studied in the time and frequency domains, the latter with orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM). Time reversal reduces the bit error rate (BER), and frequency spreading provides frequency diversity, outperforming conventional OFDM. Third, cooperative horizontal optical systems with single and multiple selective decode-and-forward relays are analysed over exponential generalized gamma turbulence. Closed-form BER and outage probability upper bound expressions are derived using Fox’s H-functions, and asymptotic analysis gives a diversity order of (K+1)/2 for K relays. Multi-relay vertical optical links are modelled with two water layers using a cascaded turbulence distribution, showing that layered channel modelling is necessary.
keywords: Underwater Wireless Communication; Underwater Acoustic Channel; Time Reversal Communication; Underwater Wireless Optical Communication; Cooperative Relaying; Exponential Generalized Gamma Turbulence; Fox’s H-Function; Bit Error Rate; Outage Probability; Diversity Order

name: Nandini Ray
thesis_title: Fluorenone based molecular scaffold: Stereoselective multicomponent synthesis, and application in asymmetric Ugi reaction
abstract:

name: Nayan Moni Baishya
discipline: School of Energy Science and Engineering
thesis_title: Few-Layer Graphene and Biomass-Derived Carbon Dot Engineered g-C3N4 Photocatalysts for Visible-Light CO2 Reduction
abstract: Photocatalytic conversion of CO2 into solar fuels offers a sustainable route to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions, but its progress is limited by rapid charge recombination and poor visible-light utilization in conventional photocatalysts. This thesis develops metal-free graphitic carbon nitride photocatalysts engineered with carbon nanomaterials to overcome these limitations. First, few-layer graphene was produced by microwave exfoliation and coupled with g-C3N4 to form composites with enhanced charge transfer and reduced energy loss. Second, carbon dots were synthesized from waste biomass, and their size was tuned to examine how particle size governs light absorption, band structure, and electron transfer. These size-controlled carbon dots were integrated with g-C3N4 to improve interfacial charge separation and photocatalytic CO2 reduction. The materials were characterized by XRD, Raman spectroscopy, XPS, BET analysis, electron microscopy, and optical studies, and their activity was evaluated in a photocatalytic reactor with product analysis by HPLC and gas chromatography. The results establish structural property and photoactivity relationships linking graphene content and carbon dot size to CO2 reduction performance. The work demonstrates that graphene and biomass-derived carbon dots are effective for designing efficient, sustainable photocatalysts for solar fuel generation.
keywords: Visible-light photocatalysis; CO2 conversion; Carbon nitride; Microwave exfoliation; Few-layer graphene; Biomass valorization; Nanomaterials synthesis; Carbon quantum dots; Solar fuels; Charge transfer; Methanol production; Carbon capture and utilization; Heterojunction; Greenhouse gas mitigation

name: Niharika Tanwar
thesis_title: Application of Pincer-Metal (Free) 3D Nano-Materials in the Electro-Catalytic Upgradation of Alcohols and Water for the Production of Hydrogen and Speciality Chemicals
abstract: My research focused on designing Pincer-Metal (Free) 3D Nano-Materials for application in alcohol-based fuel cells, as well as polymeric electrocatalysts for hydrogen production. Specifically, I have worked with Ni/Co/Cr-based bis(iminopyridine) pincer complexes and their corresponding base-metal salts for the half-cell electro-oxidation of (m)ethanol. Furthermore, these bis(iminopyridine) complexes were converted into metal oxide/hydroxide nanoparticles via a green methodology. Interestingly, these nanoparticles not only delivered high oxidation current densities but were also capable of completely oxidising alcohols to CO2 (captured as sodium carbonate), with yields of up to 98%. In addition to designing pincer metal complexes, my PhD has equipped me with polymer synthesis expertise. Using a one-pot Domino synthesis approach, metal-free and Cu-doped pincer polymers were designed for selective generation of sodium acetate from ethanol with high yields (upto 98% with PCuP-SO4), high current densities and good recyclability (cumulative 1,56,081TONs).  The metal-free pincer polymer was also used as a cathodic electrocatalyst for hydrogen production from freshwater and seawater with low energy input. The catalyst’s scope was further extended to the development of coordination polymers incorporating ?-conjugated polyaromatic hydrocarbons.  This interdisciplinary research work has strengthened my ability to connect synthesis, microscopy, and electrochemical performance evaluation across different materials platforms.
keywords: Electrocatalysis; nanomaterial designing; Polymer synthesis; Fuel cell stacking; Electrode designing; Catalysis; Battery Testing

name: Nilkamal Kalita
discipline: School of Agro and Rural Technology
thesis_title: Design and development of a ginger rhizome planter operated by a two wheel drive tractor for smallholders
abstract: Ginger cultivation is labour-intensive, particularly among smallholders in Northeast India, where traditional planting methods involve considerable drudgery. This study aimed to design, develop, and evaluate a two-wheel tractor (2WT)-operated ginger rhizome planter incorporating a dedicated metering mechanism. Five conceptual cup designs were evaluated using the AHP–TOPSIS approach, resulting in the selection of a finger-grip cup. Its dimensions were established from the physical and gravimetric properties of ginger rhizomes. A furrow opener was selected based on draft, soil disturbance, and fuel consumption, and a prototype planter was fabricated. The planter achieved an effective field capacity of 0.06 ha/h, with a theoretical capacity of 0.08 ha/h. Laboratory evaluation showed that operating speed significantly influenced seed spacing, missing index, multiple index, quality of feed index, and rhizome damage. The economic analysis indicated a break-even utilization of 64.6 h/year and a payback period of 1.16 years. Compared with manual planting, planter-assisted operation reduced working heart rate by 16.7–17.2%, oxygen consumption by 34.4–36.2%, and energy expenditure by 34.3–35.9%. RULA and REBA assessments also indicated reduced musculoskeletal risk. The developed planter offers a promising mechanization solution for reducing planting drudgery and improving ginger production efficiency among smallholders.
keywords: Ginger rhizome planter; Two-wheel tractor; Finger-grip cup metering mechanism; Agricultural mechanization; Ergonomic evaluation; Smallholder farmers.

name: Nishan Chaudhury
thesis_title: Preparation and Characterization of Kaolin Infused Tubular Membranes with Thin Zeolite Coating for Sustainable Wastewater Treatment and Heavy Metal Remediation
abstract: This research focuses on the development of low-cost, sustainable inorganic tubular ceramic membranes using naturally abundant and waste-derived materials for advanced wastewater treatment applications. Kaolin and quartz are investigated as alternative ceramic precursors, while agricultural and industrial by-products are utilized as pore-forming agents to tailor membrane porosity, pore size distribution, permeability, and mechanical strength. The fabricated membranes are systematically evaluated for microfiltration of diverse industrial wastewaters, including carwash, petroleum refinery, dairy, and oily effluents. Further surface modification using fly ash-derived zeolite is explored to enhance membrane selectivity and facilitate the removal of dissolved heavy metals and other emerging contaminants. Comprehensive physicochemical characterization, membrane performance assessment, fouling analysis, and separation mechanism investigations are undertaken to establish the membrane effectiveness in removing contaminants. Additionally, techno-economic evaluation and life cycle assessment (LCA) are incorporated to examine environmental impacts, resource efficiency, and economic feasibility. Overall, this research aims to advance affordable, resource-efficient, and sustainable ceramic membrane technologies for industrial wastewater treatment and water reuse.
keywords: Ceramic membrane; Wastewater treatment; Heavy metal treatment; Zeolite membranes; Waste valorization;

name: Niteesh Kumar
thesis_title: Performance assessment of clamshell powder based biogenic adsorbent for the treatment of waste water containing antibiotics.
abstract: Presence of antibiotics in various water bodies is a major concern for all of us as it has several harmful effect for both human and animals living there. we have attempted to remove few antibiotics such as ampicillin and tetracycline from its aqueous solution using batch adsorption method and column based method using clamshell powder based biogenic hydroxyapatite adsorbent. wet chemical precipitation method was employed for the conversion of CaO into hydroxyapatite which was further characterised using XRD, FTIR and FESEM. Both the batch adsorption and column based adsorption method showed significant removal of antibiotics from their aqueous solution. We perform proper optimisation for finding appropriate pH, temperature, adsorbent dosage and initial antibiotic concentration in case of batch adsorption while we performed optimisation of column height and flow rate in case of column based adsorption technique. Also isotherm, kinetics and thermodynamic study was performed to estimate maximum adsorption capacity, types of interaction involved, surface topology, enthalpy and gibb's free energy. similarily kinetics model such as thomas, adams bohart and yoon nelson were performed in case of column based study to investigate the column based parameters.
keywords: Waste water treatment; Antibiotics removal; Clamshell powder based adsorbent; Batch adsorption method; Fixed bed adsorption method a

name: Nuruzzaman Choudhury
discipline: School of Agro and Rural Technology
thesis_title: Assessment of solar potential and performance analysis of solar-powered systems under the climatic conditions of north-east India
abstract:
The thesis research focuses on exploring and harnessing the potential of solar energy in the northeastern region of India. To achieve this, various research objectives have been formulated to investigate the effective utilization of solar energy resources through both theoretical and experimental approaches.

A comprehensive modelling and simulation-based theoretical investigation has been carried out to evaluate the influence of various parameters on the optimal utilization of available solar energy resources by flat solar-receiving surfaces (solar PV and solar collectors).

Furthermore, an extensive performance analysis of solar-powered systems has been conducted under varying operating conditions, with particular emphasis on the prevailing climatic conditions of northeastern India.
keywords: (Solar Energy; Solar Resource Assessment; Solar Photovoltaic (PV); Solar Collector; Solar Powered Systems)

name: Pabbu Krishna Murthy
thesis_title: Computational modelling of damage evolution in elastomers and reinforced elastomeric composites
abstract:
Elastomeric composites are used in engineering applications because of their flexibility and capacity for large deformation. Predicting their response and damage evolution is challenging due to nonlinear behaviour, near-incompressibility and heterogeneous microstructure. This thesis develops a computational framework for damage and structural analysis of hyperelastic materials and particulate elastomeric composites.
First, an isotropic continuum damage model is formulated for nearly incompressible hyperelastic materials to represent progressive softening associated with polymer-chain rupture. A mixed displacement–pressure finite-element formulation incorporating the enhanced assumed strain approach addresses incompressibility. The damage evolution law is extended to different polynomial orders, and generalized displacement control is used to trace post-peak responses.
Next, composite behaviour is investigated using full-field and mean-field homogenization. Representative volume elements are generated through random sequential addition. Full-field simulations examine local field fluctuations and effective response. A second-order mean-field homogenization scheme based on the Ponte Castañeda approach estimates the effective behaviour and damage response of particulate elastomeric composites, with iterative treatment of incompressibility.Finally, the methods are applied to structural-scale problems. Comparisons of heterogeneous and homogenized descriptions assess their ability to predict overall structural response and damage evolution. The framework offers an efficient computational approach for analysing elastomeric composites across material and structural scales.
keywords: Homogenization;Damage; FEM; Nonlinear FEM; Elastomers;Elastomeric composites

name: PALADUGU RAKESH
thesis_title: Investigation of Structural Properties and Damage Mechanisms in Sustainable Polymer Composites
abstract:
