name: SHEHNAZDEEP
thesis_title: A study on effectiveness of inorganic and organic inhibitors on chloride penetration in mortar and chloride induced rebar corrosion in concrete made with geopolymer binders
abstract: Chloride-induced corrosion of steel reinforcement is a principal cause of premature deterioration in reinforced concrete structures and contributes to a global corrosion burden estimated at 3.4% of gross domestic product. Alkali-activated materials (AAMs), produced from industrial by-products, offer a markedly lower-carbon alternative to Portland cement. Their adoption in marine, deicing-salt, and sulfate-bearing environments, however, depends on their capacity to maintain the passivity of embedded steel throughout the service life. Although corrosion inhibitors are well established for Portland cement concrete, their efficacy in AAMs, whose pore solution chemistry and reaction products differ fundamentally, remains largely unverified. This study examines the performance of selected inorganic and organic inhibitors in AAM concrete exposed to chloride and composite chloride–sulfate environments. The electrochemical response of the embedded steel, characterized by half-cell potential and corrosion current density, is evaluated alongside chloride transport and correlated with strength, chloride binding, and microstructure, with an emphasis on the influence of binder chemistry on inhibitor behavior. The work provides experimental evidence to inform the selection and proportioning of corrosion inhibitors for durable, lower-carbon reinforced concrete.
keywords: Alkali-activated materials; Corrosion inhibitors; Chloride-induced corrosion; Reinforced concrete; Sulfate attack; Electrochemical characterisation; Chloride transport; Durability; Microstructural Analysis; Inhibiting Admixtures

name: Shifali Agrahari
thesis_title: AI-Generated Text Detection from Different Perspectives: A Special Focus on Text Generated by Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) generate fluent, human-like text, raising concerns about academic dishonesty, fake reviews, and misinformation. Detecting LLM-generated text remains challenging because it closely mimics human writing, while existing detectors are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, generalise poorly to unseen generators and domains, require extensive labelled data, and predominantly focus on English. This thesis addresses these challenges through supervised, few-shot, training-free, and translation-based approaches. First, we introduce three benchmark datasets: DetectAIRev for AI-generated reviews across five domains, SHAKTI for Hindi, and BHAID covering nine Indian languages. Second, we develop supervised detection methods, including stylometric analysis of human and LLM authorship, MoRE, a mixture-of-representation-experts framework designed for robustness against projected gradient descent (PGD) attacks, and DualCLF, a dual contrastive learning framework for Indian languages. Third, we propose ProtoFewRoBERTa, a prototypical few-shot approach that detects AI-generated reviews using only a limited number of labelled examples. Fourth, we introduce SeismoDet, a training-free detector that derives a physics-inspired stability score from token-level log-probability sequences. Finally, we propose TRIDENT, a round-trip translation framework for detecting AI-generated Hindi text through semantic consistency analysis. Extensive experiments demonstrate improvements over strong baselines across domains, generators, and languages, advancing robust, data-efficient, and multilingual detection of LLM-generated text.
keywords: AI-Generated Text Detection; Deepfake Detection; Large Language Models; Multilingual NLP; Natural Language Processing; Adversarial Robustness; Representation Learning; Mixture of Experts; Multimodal Learning; Computational Linguistics; Trustworthy AI

name: Shilpa Nandi
discipline: School of Interdisciplinary Studies and Sustainability
thesis_title: Autochthonous Microbial Consortia from Assam Oil Reservoirs and its Potential Application in Microbial In-situ Enhanced Oil Recovery
abstract: Microbial-enhanced oil recovery (MEOR) offers a sustainable approach for mobilizing trapped oil through microbially mediated interfacial interactions. In this study, five indigenous bacterial isolates, Bacillus subtilis SN1, B. licheniformis FD3, B. safensis ED1, B. aerius ED5, and B. safensis MD1, were selected from refinery sludge, formation water, effluent, and drilling mud based on their surface-active properties. The selected isolates demonstrated promising biosurfactant production and functional properties under challenging reservoir conditions. The produced biosurfactants exhibited effective surface and interfacial tension reduction, with structural stability and surface activity maintained at elevated temperatures (up to 90°C), salinity (10%), and pressure (3000 psi). Under oxygen-limited reservoir-simulated conditions at 60°C, biosurfactant production reached approximately 2 g/L. Core flooding experiments demonstrated additional oil recovery (AOR) of approximately 16% through ex-situ biosurfactant flooding, ~10% through in-situ microbial flooding, and ~15.0% through cyclic huff-and-puff stimulation. Biosurfactant flooding increased the capillary number approximately 74-fold and reduced the contact angle from 93° to 48°, indicating favourable wettability alteration. These findings highlight the potential of indigenous oilfield microbial isolates and their metabolites for MEOR applications through interfacial tension reduction, wettability modification, and mobilization of capillary-trapped residual oil.
keywords: Bacillus sp; Microbial Consortia; Biosurfactant; Biopolymer; MEOR; In-Situ and Ex-Situ Core Flooding; Reservoir Conditions; Oil Displacement Mechanism; Wettability Alteration

name: Shipra Aswal
thesis_title: Growth and Interface Engineering of Two-Dimensional Rhenium Dichalcogenides for Sensing, Thermal Transport, Optoelectronics, and Neuromorphic Devices
abstract: Two-dimensional rhenium dichalcogenides offer a versatile platform for investigating anisotropic physical properties and developing multifunctional electronic and optoelectronic devices. This thesis examines the growth, thermal transport, and optoelectronic properties of ReSe2 and ReS2, together with their integration into heterostructures for photodetection, reconfigurable logic, and optical synaptic applications. Chemical vapor deposition is employed to synthesize these materials, followed by structural, morphological, spectroscopic, and device characterization. Thermal transport studies investigate the influence of layer thickness and selenium vacancies on the in-plane thermal conductivity of ReSe2. Integration with silicon-on-insulator substrates enables broadband photodetection, demonstrating the importance of heterointerface engineering for optoelectronic functionality. Bi2Se3/ReS2 heterostructures exhibit electrically and optically reconfigurable bipolar photoresponse, enabling multifunctional logic operations through modulation of illumination and applied bias. The thesis further explores optical synaptic functionality in ReS2/bismuth oxyselenide heterostructures and plasma-treated ReS2, examining the effects of interface design and surface modification on light-induced conductance modulation. By connecting synthesis and materials characterization with electrical and optical measurements, this work establishes relationships between composition, defects, interfaces, and device response. These investigations advance the understanding of anisotropic layered semiconductors and identify approaches for combining photodetection, logic, and synaptic functionality within material platforms relevant to integrated optoelectronic sensing and neuromorphic information processing technologies.
keywords: Rhenium dichalcogenides; Heterostructures; Chemical vapor deposition; Thermal transport; Photodetection; Bipolar photoresponse; Reconfigurable logic; Optoelectronic synapses; Neuromorphic devices; optical synapse, TMDs.

name: Shubham Maurya
discipline: School of Interdisciplinary Studies and Sustainability
thesis_title: Design and development of a sensor integrated extrusion device for precise 3D printing of concrete structures
abstract:
The thesis focuses on the design and development of an intelligent extrusion system for automated 3D printing of reinforced concrete structures. The research aims to address key challenges in construction automation, particularly material extrusion, early-age strength development, dimensional accuracy, and reinforcement integration.

         The work involves developing a sensor-integrated extrusion device incorporating an inline mixing system for controlled admixture dosing and an automated mechanism for continuous steel cable feeding and cutting. Real-time monitoring of printing parameters and deposited layer geometry is explored to enable feedback-based process control and improve printing accuracy. Experimental investigations examine the influence of nozzle geometry, reinforcement diameter and printing parameters on extrusion performance, reinforcement integration, void formation, and structural behavior.

         The research also involves mechanical characterization through pull-out and flexural testing to evaluate reinforcement-concrete interaction and the performance of printed specimens. The project integrates mechanical design, automation, sensor integration, material characterization, experimental testing, and numerical simulation. Overall, the research advances intelligent construction technologies by developing automated, sensor-enabled extrusion systems for  concrete additive manufacturing.

name: Smrity Sonbhadra
thesis_title: Exploration of Indigenous Bacterial Communities for Biosurfactant-Mediated Bioremediation of Crude Oil Contamination
abstract: Crude oil contamination poses environmental challenges because petroleum hydrocarbons are toxic, recalcitrant, and difficult to remove in marine ecosystems. This research explores indigenous bacterial communities and their biosurfactants as sustainable tools for integrated crude oil remediation. Biosurfactant-producing bacteria were isolated from fermented food and oil-contaminated environments, characterized, and evaluated for hydrocarbon degradation and surface-active properties. Selected isolates were assembled into compatible consortia to harness complementary metabolic activities and improve remediation efficiency. A consortium demonstrated crude oil degradation, while process optimization further enhanced its performance. To address limitations of conventional treatment and slow natural attenuation, the study integrates microbial degradation with biosurfactant-assisted adsorption using modified kapok fibres, a renewable, low-cost material. The combined system was investigated under simulated seawater conditions at an enlarged experimental scale, demonstrating the potential of immobilized microbial communities to promote oil removal and hydrocarbon transformation. Hydrocarbon profiling by GC–MS assessed clhanges in aliphatic and aromatic fractions. The research also investigates an indigenous Bacillus isolate for biosurfactant production and remediation applications. Overal, this work advances an eco-friendly strategy combining microbial consortia, biosurfactants, and fibrous adsorbents. It aims to support scalable oil-spill mitigation, reduce reliance on synthetic chemicals, and contribute to sustainable marine environmental management and the circular bioeconomy.
keywords: (Bioremediation; Biosurfactants; Indigenous Bacterial Consortia; Crude Oil Degradation; Hydrocarbon Remediation; Modified Kapok Fibres; Sustainable Environmental Management; Marine Pollution)

name: Sneha Ray Barman
discipline: Centre for Linguistic Science and Technology
thesis_title: Beyond Recoverability: Diagnosing Phonological Knowledge in Neural Speech Models
abstract: Large speech models perform well on many languages, but high accuracy does not tell us whether a model has learned the grammar behind a language’s sound patterns. This research builds a diagnostic framework to separate the two, using vowel harmony in Assamese, a low-resource Indian language, as the test case. The work first built a speech corpus of 14 native speakers and established the acoustic ground truth for the vowel contrast with mixed-effects and dynamic (GAMM) models. It then tested three families of models against it. An unsupervised generative model (fiwGAN) learned the vowel categories from raw audio, with interpretable latent variables controlling the main acoustic cue, but did not coordinate vowels across a word. Probes on four self-supervised models (wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R, MMS) recovered the contrast with up to 85.8% accuracy, yet targeted tests of directionality, triggers and distance showed no rule-like behaviour. Finally, classifiers trained on human speech were used to audit two multilingual TTS systems, revealing contrast-specific errors that standard quality predictors missed. The central result is that recovering a feature from a model is not evidence that the model has learned the rule, which has direct consequences for how speech AI is evaluated.
keywords: Speech Processing; Deep Learning; Self-Supervised Speech Models; Speech Representation Learning; Model Interpretability; Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs); Multilingual Text-to-Speech (TTS) Evaluation; Acoustic Feature Analysis; Speech Corpus Development; Low-Resource Speech Technology; Computational Phonology; Assamese Vowel Harmony

name: SOHINI PAL
thesis_title: Analytical and Fractal-Geometrical Studies of Landslide-Generated Water Wave Propagation and Energy Transfer
abstract:
This research focuses on the mathematical, analytical, and computational investigation of landslide-generated water waves, emphasising wave propagation, dispersion, energy evolution, successive landslide events, porous seabed interactions, and fractal geometry. Initially, three linear water-wave models, namely fully dispersive, shallow-water, and weakly dispersive models, are considered to investigate waves generated by a submarine landslide moving horizontally at constant velocity over a porous seabed. Closed-form analytical solutions, integral representations, and far-field asymptotic approximations are developed to examine free-surface elevation, fluid velocities, resonance, and the influence of seabed permeability. The study is further extended to successive landslide events, investigating
wave interactions, amplitude variations, energy distribution, run-up, and run-down. Analytical formulations are developed to distinguish interacting and non-interacting wave fields. In addition, numerical and computational techniques, including the finite element method (FEM), are employed to investigate the governing mathematical models and their solutions. The research is subsequently extended to a fractal-dimensional framework using product-like fractal measures and local fractional operator-based methodologies to explore the influence of fractal geometry on landslide-generated wave propagation. Overall, this work integrates applied mathematics, partial differential equations, analytical and asymptotic techniques, numerical computation, fluid mechanics, and fractal geometry to develop mathematical frameworks for understanding landslide-induced tsunami dynamics and associated coastal hazards.
keywords: Landslide-generated Water Waves; FEM; Fractal Measures

name: Sonagara Abhishek Maganbhai
thesis_title: Antennas based on SSPP for B5G Radio Stripe Network application
abstract:
The deployment of Beyond 5G (B5G) networks relies on advanced architectures like cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-mMIMO) systems to ensure ubiquitous, high-capacity connectivity. A highly practical implementation approach for this is the B5G radio stripe network (RSN). This thesis presents the design, development, and experimental validation of low-cost, low-profile, and flexible microwave passive devices, specifically focusing on antennas based on spoof surface plasmon polariton (SSPP) structures. 
By leveraging uniplanar SSPP technology, the proposed designs achieve tight electromagnetic field confinement, enabling ultra-thin, highly efficient radiation characteristics suitable for conformal mounting. The research details the development of novel flexible endfire MIMO antennas and filtennas optimized for RSNs with circuit modelling. To validate their real-world applicability, the fabricated devices were rigorously measured over different surfaces, such as flat and curved brick walls and wood. 
The experimental results demonstrate that the SSPP-based antennas maintain robust impedance matching, stable radiation patterns, and high port isolation even under structural bending conditions. Ultimately, this work provides a scalable, resilient, and cost-effective physical layer solution, significantly advancing the practical deployment of flexible antenna systems for next-generation B5G radio stripe networks.
keywords: Spoof Surface Plasmon Polariton (SSPP); Beyond 5G (B5G) Radio Stripe Network (RSN); Cell-Free massive MIMO (CF-mMIMO); Uniplanar Flexible Antennas; Circuit modelling of SSPP unit cell; Endfire MIMO Antennas

name: Sonia Kahmei
discipline: Department of Humanities and Social Sciences
thesis_title: Assessing Household Energy Access and Its Determinants: A Study from Manipur, India
abstract: Ensuring universal access to modern, affordable, reliable, and sustainable energy is one of the main components of the Sustainable Development Goals. However, access to and consumption of modern energy are limited in many parts of Northeast India, particularly in geographically disadvantaged areas. This thesis investigates household energy consumption, energy choice, and transition in Manipur, comparing the hill and valley regions. It examines household energy access and consumption patterns, particularly the sources used for lighting and cooking; identifies the determinants of household energy choice; evaluates the effectiveness of government policies in promoting modern energy adoption; and assesses the impact of improved energy access on women’s autonomy within households. The study is based on primary data collected from 511 households through multistage sampling, comprising 238 households in Tamenglong (hill district) and 273 in Bishnupur (valley district). The empirical analysis employs descriptive statistics, Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression, multinomial logit regression, and propensity score matching. Although the households have access to modern energy sources, adoption of clean fuels remains low due to a range of factors, including economic conditions and cultural practices. These results underscore the need for culturally sensitive policies and for facilitating income-generating activities.
keywords: Household Energy Consumption; Energy Choice; Energy Transition; Energy Ladder Hypothesis; Fuel Stacking Hypothesis; Hill-Valley Disparities; Government Energy Policies; Women’s Autonomy; Multinomial Logit Regression; Propensity Score Matching; North East Region; India.

name: Soumya Bharadwaj
thesis_title: Fine-Grained Relation Extraction and Evaluation of Large Language Models: Resources, Error Taxonomies and Reliable Judgement
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are now widely used both to extract relational knowledge from text and to judge such outputs, yet aggregate metrics reveal little about where and why they fail. This thesis studies fine-grained relation extraction and the reliable evaluation of LLMs in four connected stages. First, it builds resources: a large relation dataset spanning 255 relation types, generated from knowledge-base tuples by combining the outputs of multiple language models. Second, it models fine-grained relations with CHART, a hierarchy-aware prompt-tuning framework trained through an LLM-judged curriculum, which outperforms twelve baselines on TACRED and a large synthetic benchmark. Third, it diagnoses errors beyond aggregate scores: ErrorBench profiles 27 LLMs from nine families in data-to-text generation using a span-level error taxonomy, and RE-ErrorTax characterises the failures of 13 LLMs across five relation extraction benchmarks for the task of zero-shot Relation extraction. Fourth, it asks whether LLMs can replace human evaluators, benchmarking LLM judges for generation and extraction against carefully annotated human labels; the judges over-diagnose errors and fall short of human agreement. Together, the thesis contributes datasets, models, error taxonomies and evaluation protocols for more trustworthy use of LLMs in building and auditing knowledge resources.
keywords: Fine-Grained Relation Extraction; LLM Evaluation; LLM-as-a-Judge; Large Language Models; Data-to-Text Generation; Error Taxonomy; Human Annotation

name: Subhadarshini Panda
thesis_title: Optimal Charging Scheduling And Coordination Approaches for Electric Vehicles in Active Power Distribution Networks Using Mixed-Integer Programming
abstract: The increasing penetration of electric vehicles (EVs) introduces complex operational challenges in power distribution networks (PDNs) due to variable charging demand, bidirectional power flows, mobility, and uncertainties. This thesis develops optimization frameworks for the coordinated integration of EVs into active PDNs by leveraging EV flexibility and network resources. Initially, a two-layer mixed-integer programming framework coordinates EV charging and discharging with dynamic distribution network reconfiguration (DNR), considering travel requirements, battery degradation, and network operating conditions. A multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming strategy further balances EV charging costs and PDN peak demand. Subsequently, a multi-layer framework integrates EV routing, charging station (CS) assignment, charging scheduling, and soft open point (SOP) operation in coupled transportation–PDN systems. To address operational uncertainties, a relative distance measure based optimization framework incorporates interval uncertainties in EV initial state of charge, traffic flow, conventional load demand, and distributed generation. Finally, a three-layer non-cooperative Stackelberg game-theoretic framework coordinates the economic decisions of PDN operators, CS operators, and EV owners. The proposed frameworks are validated on 33-bus and modified IEEE 123-bus distribution networks coupled with 41-node and 90-node transportation networks using IBM ILOG CPLEX 12.10. The results demonstrate their effectiveness in coordinated EV integration, cost management, and improved network operation.
keywords: Electric Vehicles; Charging Scheduling; Power Distribution Networks; Optimization; Mixed Integer Programming

name: Subhadip Poria
thesis_title: Exploring ferroelectric material integrated with a novel transistor for energy-efficient digital logic and gas sensing application at future technology node
abstract: This thesis focuses on the design and optimization of advanced low-power semiconductor devices for digital logic and gas-sensing applications at scaled technology nodes. Using calibrated three-dimensional TCAD simulations, the research investigates negative-capacitance field-effect transistors (NC-FETs) incorporating ferroelectric gate stacks, including MoS?-based nanosheet FETs, complementary FETs (CFETs), silicon-based nanosheet FETs, and SiGe-based vertical tunnel FETs. The study evaluates key electrical parameters, including threshold voltage, subthreshold swing, on/off-state current, output resistance, and intrinsic DC gain, to improve device performance and energy efficiency. Furthermore, CMOS inverter and ring oscillator simulations are performed to analyze circuit-level characteristics such as voltage gain, propagation delay, operating frequency, and power consumption. The research also explores NC-FET-based oxygen gas sensing through gas-induced work-function modulation and its influence on electrical sensitivity. Overall, this work demonstrates the potential of emerging ferroelectric-integrated transistor architectures for scalable, energy-efficient electronic devices and advanced gas-sensing applications.
keywords: Negative Capacitance, Nanosheet FET, Complementary FET, 2D material, Ring Oscillator, Propagation delay, Power vs Frequency

name: Subhendu Sekhar Sahu
thesis_title: Experimental and Numerical Investigation of Partial Discharge Suppression in Power Transformer Insulation Using Surface-Modified Pressboard
abstract: Partial discharge (PD) is a major degradation mechanism in power transformer insulation systems, potentially leading to progressive deterioration and eventual insulation failure. Improving the dielectric performance of pressboard insulation is therefore essential for enhancing transformer reliability. This research focuses on the development of surface-modified pressboard (SMPB) insulation to suppress partial discharge activity under high-voltage electrical stress. Initially, SMPB samples are prepared using suitable surface-modification techniques and characterized to investigate their physicochemical, morphological, and dielectric properties. Their fundamental dielectric performance is evaluated through AC breakdown voltage (ACBDV) and frequency-domain spectroscopy (FDS) measurements. Subsequently, experimental investigations are conducted to analyse PD characteristics under different AC electrical stress conditions, with particular emphasis on charge accumulation, transport, and relaxation mechanisms. Furthermore, a finite element method (FEM)-based model is developed using COMSOL Multiphysics to investigate electric-field distribution and dielectric behaviour in conventional and surface-modified pressboard insulation and validate the experimental observations. Additionally, an equivalent electrical circuit model is developed from FDS measurements to examine dielectric relaxation, interfacial polarization, and charge transport phenomena. The integrated experimental and numerical investigations aim to establish the underlying dielectric mechanisms responsible for improved insulation performance and PD suppression, demonstrating the potential of surface-modified pressboard for advanced high-voltage power transformer insulation applications.
keywords: Surface-modified pressboard; Partial discharge; Power transformer insulation; Charge dynamics; Frequency-domain spectroscopy; Dielectric relaxation; Finite element modelling; Interfacial polarization.

name: Subhojit Jash
discipline: School of Interdisciplinary Studies and Sustainability
thesis_title: Sensing beneath water: Photoplethysmography-based physiological monitoring during diving and development of an autonomous safety system for personal floatation devices
abstract: Underwater exposure induces complex cardiovascular and respiratory adaptations, necessitating reliable physiological monitoring for diver safety. This research investigated photoplethysmography (PPG)-based monitoring during SCUBA diving and developed a physiologically informed automatic inflation system for personal flotation devices. A lightweight one-dimensional convolutional neural network, Resptrack, estimated respiratory rate from PPG and was deployed on Arduino. A waterproof chest-PPG acquisition system, pressure-tested to 6 bar gauge, recorded signals from 20 certified divers during real-world dives. Heart rate agreement with a reference device and phase-dependent changes in pulse rate variability and waveform morphology were assessed. An electromechanical CO?-cartridge piercing mechanism and a multivariable drowning-risk algorithm incorporating heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and movement were developed and functionally verified. Resptrack achieved a mean absolute error of 1.94 breaths/min, increasing to 2.07 breaths/min during embedded evaluation. PPG morphology varied significantly across dive phases. The mechanism successfully pierced cartridges in ten trials, with gas-release initiation occurring within 8.75 ± 1.25 ms. These findings establish feasibility while highlighting the need for emergency-condition validation.
keywords: PPG signal; Cardiovascular and Respiratory Responses; signal processing; Machine learning; Deep learning; Drowning Risk Detection

name: Sudeepta Malakar
thesis_title: From Waste to Engineered Resource: Engineering and Environmental Evaluation of Landfill Fine Fraction for Geotechnical Applications through PPC Stabilization, Geocell Reinforcement and PLAXIS 3D Numerical Modelling
abstract: Biomining of legacy municipal solid waste generates landfill fine fraction (LFF), whose heterogeneous composition, organic matter, compressibility, and engineering properties restrict utilization. This study evaluates the geotechnical utilization of LFF recovered from the Boragaon dumpsite, Guwahati, Assam, through Portland Pozzolana Cement (PPC) stabilization, geocell reinforcement, and numerical modelling. LFF was characterized for its physicochemical, geotechnical, mineralogical, microstructural, hydraulic, and geoenvironmental properties. PPC was added at 2%, 6%, and 10%, while plate load tests assessed LFF and geocell-reinforced LFF. A finite element model was developed in PLAXIS 3D using an equivalent geocell-LFF composite-layer approach and validated against experiments. The results show that 6% PPC provides the best performance. At this dosage, CBR increased from approximately 3.7% to 41.4% under unsoaked conditions and 26.9% under soaked conditions. Effective cohesion increased from 0 to 35 kPa, while the effective friction angle increased from 35.33° to 37.32°. Geocell reinforcement improved bearing response, with the optimum configuration increasing experimental bearing pressure from 107 to 650 kPa at 10% normalized settlement. Numerical bearing pressure at 20 mm settlement increased from 80 to 652.25 kPa, while 6% PPC achieved 2166 kPa. This demonstrates LFF's potential as engineering fill and supports waste recovery, reduced disposal, and dumpsite-land reclamation.
keywords: Landfill fine fraction; Legacy waste; Portland Pozzolana Cement; Geocell reinforcement; Bearing capacity; PLAXIS 3D

name: Sujata Roy
discipline: School of Interdisciplinary Studies and Sustainability
thesis_title: Design and synthesis of Napthalene Diimide based Multipurpose fluorescent sensors for the detection of chemical and biological analytes
abstract: My doctoral research completely focuses on the design, synthesis, characterization and application of small molecule organic fluorescent probes for the detection of chemically, environmentally and biologically relevant analytes. The main objective of my thesis is to develop optical sensors which are capable to exhibit rapid and selective responses towards analytes and can be deployed to the real world to solve practical detection problems.

name: SUMANTRA CHAUDHURI
thesis_title: “Occurrence, Distribution and Impact of Microplastics in Riverine Ecosystem: Guwahati City”
abstract:
Microplastic pollution has emerged as a growing environmental concern in freshwater ecosystems, particularly in rapidly urbanizing regions. This doctoral research investigates the occurrence, spatial distribution, seasonal variability, and potential ecological impacts of microplastics in riverine environments around Guwahati, Assam, with particular emphasis on the Brahmaputra River and its associated wetland system, Deepor Beel.

The study examines microplastics in environmental samples collected across selected locations and seasons, characterizing their abundance, size, shape, and polymer composition. Analytical approaches include microscopic examination, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy, and electron microscopy, complemented by water quality assessment and spatial analysis. The research also considers the co-occurrence of microplastics and heavy metals to better understand overlapping contamination pressures. Multivariate statistical techniques and pollution risk indices are applied to investigate relationships among contamination patterns, environmental conditions, and potential ecological risks.

By integrating field observations, laboratory characterization, and quantitative assessment, the research identifies spatial and seasonal pollution patterns and evaluates possible influences of urban activities and hydrological processes. The findings provide a scientific basis for monitoring microplastic contamination, identifying vulnerable aquatic environments, and supporting evidence informed pollution management in the Brahmaputra riverine ecosystem.
keywords: Microplastic Pollution; Environmental Engineering; Riverine and Wetland Ecosystems; Water Quality Assessment; Environmental Monitoring; Pollutant Fate and Transport; Heavy Metal Contamination; Environmental Risk Assessment; Water and Sediment Analysis; Environmental Chemistry; Sustainable Water Resource Management; Statistical Data Analysis; Geospatial Analysis (GIS); Environmental Modelling; Pollution Mitigation and Remediation; Environmental Sustainability

name: Sumit Kumar
thesis_title: Development and Applications of Generalized Higher-Order Compact Methods for Unsteady Convection–Diffusion Systems
abstract: This work develops and applies generalized higher-order compact (HOC) finite-difference methods for the numerical solution of unsteady convection–diffusion systems and related fluid-flow and transport problems. The framework combines fourth-order spatial discretization with Runge–Kutta time integration, with emphasis on accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency. Starting from compact approximations for multidimensional transport equations, the formulation is extended to variable diffusion coefficients and transformed computational domains. Coordinate transformations, including sinusoidal grid stretching and body-fitted curvilinear mappings, are incorporated to represent non-uniform physical domains and improve grid resolution near boundaries and curved surfaces. The resulting discrete schemes are analysed through truncation-error derivations and stability considerations, and their accuracy is assessed using grid-convergence studies and benchmark computations. Applications include unsteady convection–diffusion problems, lid-driven cavity flow, and mixed-convection flows around circular and elliptical cylinders. The simulations are used to examine transient flow structures, vortex development, and thermal transport, including heat-transfer characteristics represented by Nusselt numbers. The study also considers the influence of governing parameters, including Reynolds, Prandtl, and Richardson numbers. Overall, the work aims to establish a unified and extensible high-order framework for transport phenomena, while providing a foundation for future extensions to implicit and IMEX Runge–Kutta time-integration strategies.
keywords: Higher-Order Compact (HOC) Methods, Convection–Diffusion Equations, Numerical PDEs, Runge–Kutta Methods, Variable Coefficients, Transformed Grids, Curvilinear Coordinates, Mixed Convection, Computational Fluid Dynamics, Heat Transfer.

name: Suraj Goala
thesis_title: Development of Predictive Models and a Multi-Physics Framework for Submerged Arc Additive Manufacturing
abstract:
Submerged Arc Additive Manufacturing (SAAM) enables high-deposition-rate fabrication of large metallic components, but its flux-covered arc and molten pool limit observation and in-situ measurement. This research develops predictive models and an integrated multi-physics framework to support process understanding, planning, and industrial implementation.

A radiation-based analytical model, incorporating a double-ellipsoidal heat-source formulation, predicts arc-column temperature and evaluates the effects of current, voltage, wire diameter, stick-out length, and deposition speed. A thermo-physical model estimates arc-induced pressure distributions and examines the influence of process parameters and material properties on molten-pool behaviour. An integrated empirical–analytical, mass-conservation-based methodology predicts beadwidth and reinforcement height through a beadwidth–reinforcement ratio. These models are validated against experimental and literature data and used for parametric and sensitivity analyses.

The research develops geometry-oriented process planning and optimisation for user-specified bead geometry and energy-efficient deposition. It assesses temperature-dependent mechanical behaviour through true stress–true strain and ultimate tensile strength predictions for intra- and inter-layer orientations, investigates surface roughness, and explores sustainable bimetallic die and mould fabrication. The models are integrated into a graphical user interface that predicts thermal, pressure, geometric, and mechanical responses from process inputs. The framework provides an efficient decision-support tool for SAAM parameter assessment, quality control, and large-scale metallic manufacturing.
keywords: Additive Manufacturing; Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing; Directed Energy Deposition; Submerged Arc Additive Manufacturing; Advanced Manufacturing; Predictive Modelling; Mathematical Modelling; Optimization; Parametric Studies; Design for Additive Manufacturing, 3D Printing, Rapid Prototyping

name: Suraj Kumar
discipline: School of Interdisciplinary Studies and Sustainability
thesis_title: Dolphin monitoring using IoT network in the river Brahmaputra
abstract: Monitoring river dolphins in freshwater environments requires reliable sensing, signal processing, and communication links that operate under underwater conditions. This work presents an integrated framework for monitoring the Ganges River dolphin in the Brahmaputra River by combining passive acoustic monitoring with underwater acoustic and optical communication. Hydrophones capture dolphin clicks and whistles alongside environmental and vessel-generated noise. Signal conditioning and machine-learning models identify dolphin vocal activity, distinguish it from interfering sounds, and extract indicators of habitat use and activity. Experimental evaluation of underwater acoustic communication based on different modulation technique. Design of low-cost solar cell-based receiver for underwater optical communication and performance evaluation of communication parameters.  Acoustic and optical links are treated as complementary technologies, with link selection guided by range, turbidity, bandwidth requirements, and deployment geometry. The framework aims to enable continuous, non-invasive dolphin observation while recording environmental conditions and human-generated noise. Integrating sensing, artificial intelligence, and communication can improve the timeliness and spatial coverage of biodiversity monitoring and provide information for conservation planning and sustainable river management.
keywords: River Dolphin Monitoring, Passive Acoustic Monitoring, Underwater Acoustic Communication, Underwater Wireless Optical Communication (UWOC), Machine Learning, Internet of Underwater Things (IoUT), Wireless communication, Embedded System

name: Suraj Kumar
thesis_title: High-Order Discontinuous Galerkin and Physics-Informed Neural Network Frameworks for Singularly Perturbed Differential Equations
abstract: Singularly perturbed differential equations arise in various physical and engineering applications and exhibit sharp boundary and interior layers that pose significant challenges for numerical approximation. My research focuses on developing robust, accurate, parameter-uniform numerical methods to solve these problems. In particular, I investigate high-order Discontinuous Galerkin finite element methods, emphasising nonsymmetric interior penalty Galerkin (NIPG) formulations, for linear and nonlinear elliptic and parabolic problems with single and multiple perturbation parameters, degenerate convection, and discontinuous coefficients. By employing layer-adapted meshes, including Shishkin, Bakhvalov–Shishkin, B-type, and exponentially graded meshes, I establish rigorous stability, well-posedness, and parameter-uniform error estimates. Furthermore, I develop superconvergence results at Gauss–Lobatto points using suitable projection and interpolation techniques. I extend these approaches to multidimensional problems using alternating direction implicit and time-fractional discretization strategies. Beyond conventional numerical methods, my research explores Physics-Informed Neural Networks and adaptive equidistributed mesh techniques for resolving sharp layers in nonlinear transport equations. The overarching objective is to develop mathematically rigorous and computationally efficient numerical frameworks for complex multiscale differential equations.
keywords: Singularly Perturbed Differential Equations; Discontinuous Galerkin Finite Element Methods; Nonsymmetric Interior Penalty Galerkin Method; Layer-Adapted Meshes; Parameter-Uniform Error Estimates; Physics-Informed Neural Networks.

name: Suranjit Basumatary
discipline: School of Agro and Rural Technology
thesis_title: Integrated IoT to Alleviate Human-Animal Conflict through Surveillance
abstract: Human-animal conflict along forest edges causes crop loss, property damage and risk to life, yet existing mitigation methods (human vigilance, fixed barriers, unmonitored camera traps) cannot combine continuous coverage with real-time response. We attempted to addresses the problem in three studies. First, ten ImageNet-pretrained CNN backbones were screened as feature extractors for 15-species classification (16,495 images). ConvNeXt-Small and EfficientNetV2-S performed best, and nested feature selection cut ConvNeXt-Small’s 768 features to 100, losing under one accuracy point. Class-conditional SHAP analysis showed features ranked low globally were critical for the hardest confusion cluster (buffalo, cow, yak), so global importance alone is an unsafe guide to dimensionality reduction. Second, a YOLOv11n detector was trained on a baseline and four rebalanced datasets (imbalance ratio 260.73) across five seeds with paired statistical testing. All strategies improved minority-class recall, but undersampling roughly halved majority-tier recall by collapsing detection attempts. Only synthetic minority augmentation gained minority recall at no detectable majority cost, a trade-off that aggregate metrics concealed. Third, these findings informed HACS, a two-tier LoRa-linked edge-AI early-warning system for off-grid sites, combining on-device detection with majority-vote confirmation, re-identification to suppress repeat alerts, severity-based escalation, automated deterrence and mobile alerts.
keywords: explainable AI; edge AI; human-wildlife conflict; early-warning system; class imbalance; transfer learning;

name: Surya veer singh pal
thesis_title: Syntheses of N-heterocycles via arene functionalization of nitrosoarenes
abstract: Indoles and their 3-substituted derivatives are always at the centre of research because of their widespread applications in pharmaceuticals as potential drug candidates and in the discovery and development of novel functional materials. In particular, the synthesis of 3-acyl indoles has drawn the immense attention of organic synthetic chemists because of their relevance in natural products and pharmaceutical entities and their capability of binding with many biological. Moreover, these 3-acylated indoles are versatile key intermediates involved in various functional group transformations to afford valuable simple to complex organic heterocyclic scaffolds. Indole is high and multi-atom nucleophil, under Friedel-Crafts acidic conditions, it suffers from competing side reactions such as 1-acylation and 1,3-diacylation, nucleophilic addition of indole to 3-acyl indole forming bis-indolyl alkanol or tris-indolyl alkane. The above methods require stoichiometric metal salt as Lewis acid promoters and strict exclusion of moisture. however, these Lewis acids suffer one or more disadvantages such as commercial non-availability, cost, toxicity, handling difficulty/hazards, non-feasibility toward various substituted/functionalized acylating reactants, and the inconvenience of the procedure, especially extraction difficulty of the reaction mixture Therefore, the synthesis of 3-acyl indoles is still of great research interest. Herein, we report an acid-catalyzed annulation reaction of ?-amino carbonyl compound and nitrosoarenes to provide 3-acyl indole derivatives without using any metal catalysts and oxidant.

name: Susmita Bhattacharjee
thesis_title: Fairness-Aware and Efficient Speech Foundation Models for Pathological Speech Recognition and Severity Assessment
abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems trained predominantly on typical speech often exhibit degraded performance for individuals with cleft lip and palate (CLP), particularly across varying impairment severities. This thesis investigates inclusive speech technologies through interconnected studies addressing severity assessment, recognition fairness, cross-severity adaptation, and edge deployment. Initially, pretrained speech foundation models, including Whisper, Wav2Vec2, and WavLM, are evaluated for CLP detection and severity classification. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning using LoRA and DoRA improves classification performance while reducing trainable parameters. Subsequently, a severity-aware data-mixing strategy progressively incorporates pathological speech into ASR training, improving recognition accuracy and the accuracy–fairness trade-off between Normal and CLP speech. Phoneme-level analysis further examines recognition errors across different articulation categories. To enhance cross-severity generalization, a Normal-Anchored First-Order Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (NA-FOMAML) framework is proposed, demonstrating improved recognition performance and fairness compared with conventional severity-aware fine-tuning. Additional investigations examine adaptation strategies and encoder behavior to understand pathological speech representation learning. Finally, Whisper-based models are deployed on NVIDIA Jetson hardware, demonstrating real-time inference and improved recognition performance without increasing inference-memory requirements. Overall, this research advances accurate, fairness-aware, computationally efficient, and deployable speech recognition technologies, contributing toward more accessible and inclusive speech-based human–computer interaction for individuals with CLP.
keywords: Speech Signal Processing; Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR); Speech Foundation Models; Pathological Speech Detection and Severity Assessment; Deep Learning; Machine Learning; Speech Representation Learning; Transformer-Based Models; Transfer Learning; Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT); LoRA and DoRA; Meta-Learning; Domain Adaptation; Fairness-Aware AI; Robust Speech Recognition; Generative AI; Edge AI; Model Training and Optimization; Real-Time Speech Processing; AI for Healthcare

name: Swati Upadhyay
thesis_title: Durability and Security of Emerging Non-Volatile Memories
abstract: Emerging Non-Volatile Memories (NVMs) like Phase-Change Memory (PCM) offer attractive byte-addressability, non-volatility, and near-zero standby power as high-density main memory alternatives to traditional DRAM, which faces severe scaling walls. However, their physical vulnerability to high write energy and latency, limited cell write endurance, write disturbance errors, susceptibility to non-volatile data remanence attacks and crash consistency anomalies impede widespread commercial deployment. To overcome these limitations, this research proposes novel microarchitectural optimizations, including efficient compression, wear-leveling, and adaptive data encoding to reduce costly writes, improve NVM lifetime, and mitigate write disturbance errors, and provide efficient encryption to secure non-volatile data without affecting lifetime, while ensuring crash consistency in systems integrating memory encryption and integrity verification into the memory hierarchy. Through rigorous cycle-accurate simulation and workload evaluation using gem5 and NVMain, this work demonstrates that intelligent microarchitectural co-design simultaneously extends NVM lifespan, secures stored data against security threats, and preserves system performance while ensuring crash consistency, paving the way for resilient next-generation computer memory systems.
keywords: Non-Volatile Memory; Phase-Change Memory; Microarchitectural Optimizations; Memory Security; Memory Encryption; Cycle-Accurate Simulation; Bit-flips, Memory Lifetime, Encoding, Compression, Wear Leveling, Write Disturbance Error, Bonsai Merkle Trees

name: TANUSREE GHOSHAL
thesis_title: Point-of-Care Biosensors for Early Detection of Cardiac, Pancreatic, Thyroid and Inflammatory Illnesses
abstract: With the ever-present and increasing burdens of both communicable and noncommunicable diseases, the necessity for facile, readily available diagnostic technologies could not be more apparent or urgent. Therefore, my thesis aims to explore a few methodologies to detect biomarkers in serum, which may be translated to point-of-care testing devices for use at either the patients’ site or in primary health care centres. The objectives of my thesis delineate the detection of a few inherent health issues and diseases, which may be indicated by anomalies in the levels of certain biomarkers in the serum. The biomarkers investigated herein include Pancreatic Lipase, Serum Triglyceride, Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone, and Cortisol. My thesis explores a multitude of detection methodologies including Colorimetry, Analytical Electrochemistry, and UV-Vis Spectroscopy, all of which may be translated to Point-of-Care diagnostic platforms using miniaturized technologies such as microfluidics and portable analytical instruments. Herein, the efficacy and sensitivity of each detection protocol have been thoroughly established, along with the simplicity of their development and deployment. Thus, my thesis presents multiple prototypes for multimodal point-of-care detection platforms which can be deployed to analyse the levels of biomarkers in human serum.
keywords: Biosensor; Nanoparticles; Colorimetry; Plasmonics; Electrochemistry; Point-of-care Testing; Prototype Development;

name: Toni Kumari
thesis_title: Experimental Investigation of Startup and Transient Characteristics of Miniature Loop Heat Pipe
abstract: The electronics and data centres are intensifying the challenge of thermal management. The doctoral research focused on the experimental study and mathematical modelling of miniature loop heat pipes (MLHP), with the goal of making this passive cooling technology more reliable and practical for real-world, miniaturized applications. The work spanned materials development, system-level modelling, and hands-on experimental testing. The research began with the in-house fabrication of advanced porous wick structures, the components responsible for capillary pumping and circulating fluid within the system. These wicks were then thoroughly characterized to understand their structural and capillary properties, directly addressing two persistent challenges such as excessive pressure drop within the evaporator, and heat leak, that affects system efficiency. By introducing bi-porous wick structures, along with composite wicks, both problems were successfully resolved. Building on these characterization results, MLHP prototypes were developed and fabricated, with evaporator designs and wick configurations selected based on what the earlier characterization had shown to perform best. Several such configurations were built, tested, and compared to identify what worked best under realistic operating conditions. With the prototypes in hand, detailed experimental studies were then carried out to understand how these systems started up, stabilized, and performed under steady operating conditions.
keywords: Miniature Loop Heat Pipe; Thermal Management; Electronics Cooling; Sintered Porous Wick; Startup Characteristics; Steady-State Performance; IR Visulization

name: Udangshree Borah
discipline: School of Interdisciplinary Studies and Sustainability
thesis_title: Sustainable Development of Spirulina-Based Protein Ingredients and Functional Foods: Protein Recovery, Functionalization, Product Development and Environmental Assessment
abstract:
The growing demand for sustainable and nutritious food ingredients has encouraged research into alternative protein sources and resource-efficient processing technologies. Thus, my doctoral research investigates the recovery, functionalization, and food applications of Spirulina (Arthrospira platensis) proteins, integrating ingredient functionality with environmental sustainability.
Conventional alkaline and deep eutectic solvent-based extraction methods, with and without ultrasound assistance, are evaluated for protein recovery, physicochemical characteristics, techno-functional properties, and environmental impacts through life cycle assessment. Protein solubility, emulsifying properties, water and oil holding capacities, structural characteristics, and in vitro digestibility are examined to assess application potential.
The research further explores protein-polyphenol interactions to develop functional ingredient systems for emulsion-based formulations and structured food products. A circular bioeconomy approach is examined through valorization of protein-extraction residual biomass into functional snack bars, with evaluation of nutritional composition, product quality, safety, and in vitro digestion-related properties.
Collectively, the work aims to connect sustainable protein processing, ingredient functionality, and food product development, supporting the design of value-added food ingredients while reducing biomass waste and environmental burdens.
keywords: Food Product Development; Food Formulation; Alternative Proteins; Protein Extraction and Functionality; Functional Food Ingredients; Protein-Polyphenol Interactions; Emulsion Technology; Process Optimization; Biomass Valorization; Life Cycle Assessment

name: Udit Kumar
thesis_title: Residual Stress Study in Metal Additive Manufacturing: Integrating Characterization, Uncertainty Quantification, Mitigation Strategies, and Computationally Efficient Prediction Method
abstract: Residual stress is a critical concern in metal additive manufacturing (AM), influencing dimensional accuracy, structural integrity, mechanical performance, and component reliability. The complex thermal cycles, rapid solidification, and repeated heating and cooling inherent to metal AM processes generate non-uniform residual stress distributions, making their accurate assessment and control challenging. This research presents an integrated approach to residual stress characterization, uncertainty quantification, mitigation, and computationally efficient prediction in metal AM, with particular emphasis on wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM). Experimental investigations focus on residual stress distribution under different processing conditions, supported by microstructural and mechanical characterization. A geometry-aware measurement framework is developed to improve the reliability of X-ray diffraction-based residual stress measurements on non-uniform surfaces through uncertainty quantification and optimized measurement strategies. Furthermore, process optimization and thermal management strategies are investigated to mitigate residual stresses and improve manufacturing integrity. Machine learning (ML) techniques will be employed to develop computationally efficient predictive models, establishing relationships between processing parameters, material characteristics, and residual stress distributions while reducing dependence on computationally intensive numerical simulations. The research aims to establish a comprehensive framework for reliable residual stress assessment, effective mitigation, and ML-based prediction, contributing to improved process control and structural reliability of metal AM components.
keywords: Residual Stress; Metal Additive Manufacturing; Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM); X-ray Diffraction (XRD); Uncertainty Quantification; Residual Stress Mitigation; Machine Learning; Predictive Modeling

name: Vamsi Krishan Gali
thesis_title: Seismic Analysis and Design of URM Buildings with Curved Walls
abstract: My doctoral research investigates the seismic behavior of curved masonry walls, both as isolated components and within unreinforced masonry (URM) buildings, through experimental and numerical studies. Shake-table tests on scaled specimens and quasi-static reverse-cyclic tests on full-scale specimens evaluated dynamic characteristics, lateral resistance, deformation, and failure mechanisms. Isolated walls predominantly exhibited base flexural cracking and rocking, whereas curved walls incorporated into URM buildings developed diagonal shear cracking and vertical splitting. Nonlinear finite element models were developed in Abaqus and validated against experimental results. Parametric studies showed that lateral load-carrying capacity increased with wall thickness, masonry strength, axial stress, and height at constant aspect ratio, but decreased with increasing aspect ratio. Drift capacity generally increased with aspect ratio and thickness but decreased with masonry strength and height-to-thickness ratio. Empirical equations were developed to predict the lateral load-carrying capacity, base shear coefficient, and drift capacity of curved masonry walls. Comparative numerical studies examined differences in lateral behavior between URM buildings incorporating curved walls and conventional box-type URM buildings. The radius of curvature was also varied to assess its influence. Results demonstrated that building configuration and curved-wall geometry influenced stiffness, lateral resistance, deformation capacity, and failure mechanisms.
keywords: Masonry Structures; Curved Masonry Walls; Seismic Analysis; FE Modelling

name: Vandana Kumari
thesis_title: Resilience-oriented investment and operational planning of active power distribution networks using mixed-integer programming
abstract: My PhD thesis presents investment and operational planning approaches for enhancing the resilience of power distribution networks (PDNs) under extreme weather events. First, a multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model is developed to coordinate the operation of mobile emergency generators (MEGs) and network reconfiguration (NR), minimizing load shedding and load restoration costs. Subsequently, a two-stage stochastic MILP model is formulated to determine optimal investments in MEGs and repair crews (RCs) under uncertain line-damage scenarios. A progressive hedging-based solution approach is developed to solve the stochastic planning problem. Furthermore, an integrated PDN and transportation network model is developed to optimize MEG routing, line-repair crew scheduling, road-clearing crew scheduling, and NR. Finally, an information-gap decision theory (IGDT)-based model is developed to address uncertainties in renewable generation and load demand without requiring known probability distributions. The model coordinates MEGs, photovoltaic units, wind turbines, battery energy storage systems, and NR under risk-averse and risk-seeking strategies. An augmented epsilon-constraint method and fuzzy decision-making approach are employed to obtain Pareto-optimal solutions and select the best solution. The proposed approaches are validated on standard 33-bus and modified IEEE 123-bus test systems.
keywords: Resilience; Load Restoration; Operation Planning; Investment Planning; Active Power Distribution Networks; Optimization; Stochastic Modeling; Uncertainties; Transportation Network; Distributed Energy Resources; Mixed-integer Linear Programming; Mathematical Modeling; Information Gap Decision Theory; Interval Arithmetic; Multi-objective Optimization; K-means Clustering Method

name: Vijaya
discipline: School of Energy Science and Engineering
thesis_title: Development of carbon-coated silicon graphite composite anode and its application in lithium-ion batteries
abstract: The growing demand for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) has driven research into silicon–graphite composite anodes. This thesis investigates carbon-coated silicon–graphite composites containing 10%, 12% and 15% silicon, synthesized through liquid-phase solidification using coal tar pitch as a carbon precursor. Electrochemical evaluation demonstrates initial discharge capacities of approximately 558, 796 and 809 mAh g?¹, respectively, with capacity retentions of 87.44%, 72.03% and 68.35% after 100 cycles. The 12% silicon composite anode, further evaluated in an NMC811 full cell, delivers an initial discharge areal capacity of approximately 2.5 mAh cm?². A two-level stacked ensemble model integrating Random Forest, Gradient Boosting and XGBoost is developed for battery state-of-health (SoH) prediction and compared with an artificial neural network (ANN) model. Evaluation across 14 diverse battery datasets yields prediction error below 3%, demonstrating good predictive capability. Finally, a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) of 1 kWh NMC-based LIBs containing the developed composite anode examines the influence of silicon content, battery capacity and electricity sources on environmental impacts. The findings highlight the benefits of higher-capacity anodes and lower-carbon electricity. Overall, this research integrates material development, battery health prediction and environmental assessment to advance high-performance and sustainable LIB technologies, supporting SDGs and battery passports.
keywords: lithium-ion batteries; silicon anode; silicon graphite anode; NMC; cathode; battery fabrication; energy storage; electrochemical characterization; electrochemical impedance spectroscopy; material characterization; life cycle assessment; sustainability; clean energy; electric vehicles; batterypacks;

name: Vinny Kohli
discipline: School of Agro and Rural Technology
thesis_title: Development and Partial Techno-Functional Characterization of RTE Baked Products Prepared from Two Selected Whole Legumes
abstract: Legumes are sustainable, nutrient-dense sources of plant protein; however, conventional fractionation involves energy-intensive operations and generates waste. This study aimed to develop ready-to-eat baked snacks from whole lentil and soybean seeds using an integrated, minimally processed approach. Multivariate statistical techniques were employed to select protein-rich raw materials based on proximate composition and amino acid profiles. Standardised soaking and cooking facilitated hydration, softening, and formation of cohesive, binder-free doughs. Integration of wet milling, cold extrusion, and controlled drying enabled whole-legume snack production while eliminating dehulling and minimising losses. The developed snacks offered an alternative to deep-fried Bhujia, with higher protein and dietary fibre, reduced fat, and acceptable sensory characteristics. Air-frying emerged as a time-efficient alternative to tray drying while maintaining product quality and storage safety. Structural and physicochemical characterisation revealed processing-induced matrix modifications without substantial changes to primary molecular functional groups. Simulated gastrointestinal digestion demonstrated effective protein hydrolysis and nutrient solubilisation. Furthermore, fermentation with Bacillus subtilis BS1747 MTCC enhanced matrix disintegration, protein digestibility, and nutrient bioaccessibility through enzymatic modification. Soluble and insoluble solids measurements showed potential as indicators of digestibility. Overall, this study establishes a sustainable strategy for converting whole legumes into value-added snacks, with applications in small-scale food industries.
keywords: Pulses; Snacks; Traditional Processing; Cold-Extrusion; Tray-Drying; Air-Frying; Whole Seed; Microstructure; Texture; Protein; Protein Solubility; Protein Digestibility; Nutrition; Value addition

name: Vishal Dhar
thesis_title: Application of Foam-based CO2-Enhanced Oil Recovery for Northeast Indian Oil Fields
abstract: The research focuses on foam-based CO2-enhanced oil recovery (EOR) and geological CO2 sequestration, with particular emphasis on developing sustainable strategies for simultaneous hydrocarbon recovery and subsurface carbon storage in mature oilfields of Northeast India. Conventional CO2 gas injection faces challenges associated with viscous fingering, gravity override, and premature gas breakthrough, which limit sweep efficiency and storage potential. The research explores stabilized CO2 foam and microbubble systems as promising alternatives for improving gas mobility control, displacement efficiency, and CO2 retention in heterogeneous sandstone reservoirs. The study involves nanoparticle-assisted CO2 foam generated using natural and bio-based surfactants, with emphasis on understanding their physicochemical interactions. The research investigates the influence of surfactant-nanoparticle systems on interfacial tension, wettability alteration, foam stability, bubble dynamics, rheological behaviour and oil recovery. Furthermore, experimental data was validated using CMG software and used to generate reservoir scale model for efficient CO2 utilization, and storage performance. Ultimately, the research aims to establish an integrated framework for efficient CO2-EOR and geological sequestration in Northeast Indian reservoirs.
keywords: Enhanced Oil Recovery; CO2 Storage; CCUS; Reservoir Simulation

name: Vivekananda G
thesis_title: Energy-Efficient Implementation of Lightweight Cryptographic Techniques Using Approximate Computing
abstract: Resource-constrained IoT and embedded devices need cryptographic protection under tight latency, energy and area budgets. Lightweight ARX (Addition-Rotation-XOR) primitives suit these platforms, but carry propagation in modular adders limits their hardware throughput and energy efficiency. Approximate computing can shorten this critical path, but careless approximation introduces exploitable structural weaknesses. This research develops cryptography-aware approximate adders that approximate only the carry logic, preserving the nonlinearity and bit diffusion that modular addition provides. Carry-limited adders restrict propagation to the preceding 1–4 bits, giving constant-time carry computation. A spatially permuted variant breaks rotational symmetry to resist rotational cryptanalysis, and a reversibility-preserving variant supports block ciphers. These adders are integrated into five accelerators: ChaChAx (stream cipher), HAxSH and ELMAA (PRF/MAC), AxLEA (block cipher) and AEAx (authenticated encryption). Security is validated through avalanche analysis, ENT, NIST STS, DieHarder, and MILP-based linear, differential and rotational cryptanalysis, and the designs are implemented on ASIC and FPGA platforms. ChaChAx uses up to 70% less energy, HAxSH has 6× lower latency, AxLEA gains about 5× in energy, latency and throughput, and AEAx consumes 0.58 pJ/bit. This work establishes approximation as a practical hardware acceleration technique for lightweight cryptography.
keywords: Hardware security, Cryptography, Computer Architecture, Lightweight Cryptography

name: Yengkhom Omesh Singh
thesis_title: Seismocardiography-Based Non-Invasive Cardiac Assessment Through Waveform Characterization and Morphological Analysis
abstract: This research focuses on the development of signal processing and machine learning approaches for non-invasive cardiac assessment using seismocardiography (SCG), a technique that captures chest-wall vibrations associated with cardiac mechanical activity. The primary objective is to investigate SCG waveform characteristics for cardiac event identification, physiological parameter estimation, and morphology-based assessment of cardiac conditions. The work encompasses SCG signal preprocessing, waveform delineation, and detection of cardiac fiducial points, particularly aortic valve opening, using techniques such as linear prediction coding and other advanced signal processing methods. Furthermore, SCG morphological variations are investigated to characterize cardiac activity and identify physiological and pathological changes. Machine learning and deep learning frameworks are developed to interpret SCG signals for cardiac assessment, including respiratory state identification and heart failure detection. Particular emphasis is placed on multiaxial SCG analysis to exploit complementary information across the three accelerometer axes and improve the characterization of cardiac mechanical activity. The overall research aims to establish reliable, non-invasive, and computationally efficient methods for extracting meaningful cardiac information from SCG waveforms, thereby contributing to wearable cardiac monitoring and intelligent assessment of cardiovascular function.
keywords: Biomedical Signal Processing; Deep Learning; Patern Recognition;  Physiological Signal; Time Series Signal, Edge AI, Tiny ML
